📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it was 5:55 a.m. on Friday when the Bundestag's Budget Committee concluded its final session.

Following nearly 16 hours of negotiations, lawmakers from the conservative Christian Democratic Union(CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) parties, along with their coalition partners from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), voted in favor of the 2027 draft budget. The opposition parties — the environmentalist Greens, the socialist Left Party and the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) — voted against it. With that, the way is now clear for the final vote in the Bundestag on November 27.

Reading through the nearly 1,000-page document requires a great deal of number-crunching. Next year, the federal government plans to spend around €561 billion ($620 billion).

Industry observers note that but here's the problem: it won't collect nearly enough revenue to cover these expenses. With a shortfall of €123 billion, borrowing will be needed to bridge the gap.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that but that's not the only problem. On top of all this debt, Germany also has loans for defense spending and for the renovation of the dilapidated infrastructure. Approved by the Bundestag in 2025, these special funds are set to be in place for multiple years.

If the new debt for 2027 is factored in, the total borrowing amounts to over €210 billion. This is the second-highest level of borrowing in the history of the Federal Republic of Germany. The only time Germany borrowed more was during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021, when borrowing reached €215.4 billion.

Industry observers note that this development has drawn sharp criticism from opposition parties. Green Party lawmaker Sebastian Schäfer and his colleague Dietmar Bartsch of the Left Party called it a "gigantic mountain of debt," an "untrustworthy" budget, "irresponsible" policies at the expense of future generations and a lack of future prospects.

To understand the reasons behind the growing debt, one has to look beyond the numbers. Every federal budget is a snapshot of the priorities set by a government and a country — in terms of the economy, social complications, security and geopolitics.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

For 2027, that story continues to be one of crises and wars. While Russia's war against Ukraine is driving up defense spending, the faltering economy is also demanding new investments. At the same time, Germany's population is aging rapidly, which is driving up social spending.

What's more, the crumbling infrastructure must be repaired and modernized, and the energy transition is costing billions. And more than half of all this debt is going toward security and defense.

Sources indicate that russia's war against Ukraine will enter its sixth year in 2027. As of the end of June, the federal government estimated its overall support for Ukraine to have reached approximately €100 billion. In response to a request from the AfD in the Bundestag, the government stated: "The federal government will continue to provide Ukraine with political, financial, humanitarian, civil and military support for as long as necessary.".

The rearmament of the Bundeswehr and spending on NATO are also putting massive pressure on the budget. The defense budget is set to grow to just under €110 billion in 2027, an increase of around €27 billion compared to last year. Added to this are expenditures from the Bundeswehr's special fund.

Recent findings suggest that nevertheless, by far the largest single budget item comes from the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs, which is set to grow to over €200 billion. There are intends for cost-cutting measures, for example, in basic income support for job seekers. But the costs of old-age pension benefits continue to rise.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that people born in the 1960s have begun to retire. Back then, more than 1 million children were born each year. But birth rates nearly halved in the early 1970s and have continued to decline since then. As a result, there will be an increasing number of retirees and a decreasing number of working-age individuals in the coming years.

The pension funds cannot be financed by the pension contributions of this dwindling workforce and have to be subsidized by the government. Already, contributions to the pension insurance system — which are split equally between employees and employers — will have to be increased. They are expected to rise to just under 20% of gross salary.

In a recent development, the Federal Employment Agency, too, has long been unable to make ends meet on contributions alone. In 2027, subsidies of more than €8 billion from the federal budget are planned.

It has been revealed that anyone comparing Germany's current budget situation with that of past years will be rubbing their eyes in disbelief. It wasn't that long ago that Germany was considered a model of fiscal discipline. Between 2014 and 2019, the federal budget managed to avoid taking on latest debt for six consecutive years. In some years, there was even money left over.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that but the era of "balanced budgets" came to an abrupt end with the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. However, today Germany is still enjoying the benefits of those years of fiscal stability. Compared to other countries, Germany is still in relatively good shape.

The key indicator is not the amount of debt along but the debt-to-GDP ratio. It indicates how high the national debt is in relation to annual economic output.

It has been revealed that at the end of 2025, it stood at 63.5% for Germany. France, on the other hand, stands at over 110% and Italy at about 135% to 140%, while the US is well above 100%. However, in its latest fall report, the German Council of Economic Experts warned that Germany could be heading down a dangerous path. If debt continues to rise at this rate, the debt-to-GDP ratio could climb to 100% by 2040.

Recent findings suggest that this would also put Germany's creditworthiness on the financial markets at risk. Germany is the only country among the seven leading democratic industrialized nations (G7) that still holds a triple-A (AAA) rating. This is the highest possible credit rating on the financial markets. It signals to investors that the risk of default on German government bonds is extremely low.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Recent findings suggest that this also means that interest rates on new loans are not set as high. This is an important point, as interest payments place an increasing burden on the federal budget each year. By 2027, approximately €42 billion in interest payments are expected to be due.

At the end of November, the Bundestag will hold its final debate on the draft budget. Should changes be expected by then? There is disagreement within the government over whether a reduction in the electricity tax might still be possible.

The prospect of such a reduction had been raised by Chancellor Friedrich Merz. On Friday, during a European leaders summit in Dublin, he reiterated: "I expect that we will discuss this again next Tuesday in the coalition committee, and I remain committed to my goal of lowering the electricity tax to the European minimum — in full — starting next year.".

While the head coach, players and Spanish press were magnanimous in defeat, there was pride mixed in with disappointment – and confidence the future is still bright.

It has been revealed that “With every game, defeat gets closer,” Luis de la Fuente had said and on Sunday night it finally came. Spain had lost only one competitive game since Scotland in March 2023 back when the coach hadn’t won anything and didn’t look like he ever would – and that solitary loss was on penalties in the 2025 Nations League final. Statistically, they said, penalties don’t count, so while Portugal lifted the trophy that night, the team that won the European Championship and World Cup in the summers either side also claimed a Fifa record of 44 official games unbeaten. And then England turned up at the Metropolitano.

Industry observers note that A night that started with Iker Casillas, Fernando Torres and Fernando Llorente handing the World Cup to Unai Simón ended with Spain trying to overhaul a shock 3-0 deficit. Against 10 men and led by a superb Lamine Yamal, Spain made De la Fuente think for a while that they would too, but it wasn’t to be.

Recent findings suggest that aymeric Laporte had almost levelled it in the 91st minute, denied by James Trafford. “I thought it was in, but that’s football,” the defender said, and in football some days you lose, especially against opponents such as these. “This could have been the World Cup final,” the coach said.

Had it been, who knows, this might have been different. From a Spanish perspective, better to lose now, with both teams already through to the Nations League quarter‑finals, than somewhere else: better than Berlin, June 2024, that’s for sure. There might even have been some value in it, the coach welcoming a glimpse of “reality” and claiming that everything he took from the defeat was positive. Thomas Tuchel had said Spain can look “invincible” but sometimes it helps to be reminded you’re not. Which isn’t to say they wanted it to happen now, still less that they didn’t care. “It’s a pity,” Mikel Oyarzabal said. “It hurts,” Simón admitted. “But we knew at some point it could happen.”.

According to recent reports, not that the analysis ends there. Before the game Simón had lifted the trophy in the absence of Rodri, who was replaced by Martín Zubimendi. And although De la Fuente likes to say that Zubimendi is the second-best central midfielder in the world after the captain, although Zubimendi was on the pitch when they won the European Championship and the World Cup, he has not started a Premier League game for Arsenal and faced Declan Rice, who has started 10. “Sometimes it’s not easy to come to the national team when you’re not playing many minutes,” Zubimendi had accepted after a narrow win against Czechia three days earlier. There was also a start for Mikel Merino too, often the supersub. And not for Pedri.

Recent findings suggest that asked about Pedri’s absence, De la Fuente shot back: “Fabián’s not a bad player either, is he?” The past two tournaments have ended with Pedri losing out – to Dani Olmo at No 10 at Euro 2024 and to Fabián Ruiz in central midfield at the World Cup. They have also ended with Spain winning the titles, the decision justified; the Barcelona midfielder has begun only two of the past nine matches for Spain, and they have won eight. Yet the continued absence of a midfielder who may be the most talented in the team is disconcerting, maybe even feels like a defeat in itself. At the Metropolitano it was in midfield, unusually, where Spain did not take control and he helped change the game when introduced.

According to recent reports, de la Fuente also admitted that Spain had been struggling from dead balls – in fact that was part of the reason to include Marc Pubill and Merino. That has been a constant since the World Cup, Simón said, and it showed on the second goal. Olmo was absent. It was not easy to live with the intensity England imposed. And Laporte called it a “peculiar” week: he had missed Prague with a virus that others had feared catching too. There had also been the debate about Lamine Yamal before the game, and none whatsoever about him after it.

Yet more than the analysis, much of which will have morphed by March when the national team meet up again, there was a certain acceptance. Appreciation too, for Spain and for their opponents. “After three years and 44 games unbeaten, it would be a bit strange to say: ‘This has to change.’ I don’t feel that way at all,” De la Fuente noted, and everyone agreed.

Recent findings suggest that what happened? England happened. “The second-best team in the world, comparable to us,” as Simón called them. Oyarzabal talked about how Tuchel’s team had gone man to man all over the pitch, a team of “clear ideas”. Laporte spoke of how deeply they had studied Spain. “They overran us in the first 30 minutes, they were superior throughout most of the game … and we still nearly turned it around,” De la Fuente said.

No excuses: England were just better, “a formidable opponent: voracious, ambitious, scorching”, in El País’s words. “If you’re going to lose your run, better to do it against an imposing opponent like England,” said Marca. Spain were “obliged to recognise they had a stupendous rival before them, defeat is not unjust”, El Mundo wrote.

Industry observers note that “This can happen against England,” Simón remarked. It was just that they had “forgotten what defeat tastes like”, De la Fuente admitted, and while that wasn’t nice it was also something of which to be proud.

“This serves to underline what we have done,” he repeated over and over and over again; it served to value a record-breaking run, the trophies won en route and what lies ahead.

It was time to build towards another record but that didn’t mean beginning again, it meant carrying on. “The best is yet to come,” De la Fuente said. “This shows how hard it is to get here. As they say: ‘Let’s see you beat that.’”.

Sources indicate that at the end of the match, De la Fuente lined up alongside his staff and applauded his players off the pitch, a guard of honour for the men who had made history. “In the dressing room they were sad,” he noted. “But I told them: ‘Gentlemen, do you know what you’ve done? Do you know where we are? This is historic. Let’s see if anyone ever matches this. Maybe they will … or maybe they won’t.’”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The assistant referee had a 60-day recovery period after being operated on.

An Ecuadorian footballer has been banned for eight years for throwing a rock at an assistant referee, leaving him requiring surgery to his face.

Jhon Perlaza was playing for Club Ciudad de Yantzaza against Club Rio Aguarico FC in a third-tier match in October when the incident took place.

The stone struck assistant referee Lenin Giovanni Ojeda Nunez in the face in the 96th minute of the game, which was subsequently abandoned.

A video on social media shows Perlaza standing up in the team's dugout to throw the stone, with Nunez instantly falling to the floor and holding his face after the object hits him. He then receives medical attention.

"The assistant referee suffered serious injuries that required surgery and a 60-day recovery period," the Ecuadorian Football Federation (FEF) mentioned.

"The disciplinary committee found the player responsible for physical aggression against a match official and suspended him for eight years from all football-related activity, until 19 October, 2034.

"In addition, the FEF will ask Fifa to extend this sanction worldwide.".

The FEF also fined his club Yantzaza $2,000 (Â£1,521) and ordered them to pay Nunez's medical fees of $4,369 (Â£3,323).

In a statement released on 20 October, three days after the match, Yantzaza apologised to the refereeing team and the fans, and confirmed Perlaza had been sacked as a result of the incident.

"As an institution, we categorically reject all acts of aggression, whether verbal or physical, both inside and outside sporting venues. We firmly believe that football should be a space of respect, coexistence, and fair play," they said.

"Once the person responsible for this regrettable incident was identified, the institution made the decision to remove him immediately, and he is therefore no longer part of our club.".

Are Liverpool prepared for Grand Theft Auto to ruin their weekend preparation?

Ah s***, here we go again: GTA VI dropped this week to rapturous acclaim from critics and public alike, with the long-awaited video game responsible for plenty of us turning up to work a little bleary-eyed after an all-nighter in Vice City.

And given that Premier League footballers are often avid gamers – they have a lot of time on their hands – FPL players are going to have to take into account those last-minute “groin strains” that see big-hitters pull out of this weekend's action….

In September 2013, Liverpool defender Daniel Agger suffered a freak abdominal injury when he overstretched to prevent a dumbbell from falling on his foot in training. Or did he?

No, he probably did: but while the story certainly made sense – and Agger even aggravated the injury after playing through the pain barrier – the fact that Grand Theft Auto V was released that week certainly led some to wonder whether the Dane had in fact pulled a sickie.

Agger was far from the only suspicious absentee that week in the league either, with high-profile names missing up and down the country.

Robin van Persie and David Silva both missed the Manchester derby, completely unexpectedly, with the stars ruled out late with sudden muscle injuries: Manchester United boss David Moyes even revealed that he'd given RVP the chance to play right up until that Sunday morning.

Theo Walcott was even named in Arsenal's starting line-up for Stoke City that weekend, but pulled out with a mysterious “abdominal matter”, paving the way for Serge Gnabry to step in, while Gareth Bale was expected to make his Real Madrid debut that weekend, only for a “thigh tweak” in the warm-up to rule him out.

Silva and Walcott both missed the following fixtures – suggesting they really did have an alibi, with the latter requiring surgery – though Van Persie and Bale both recovered to make the bench the following week (convenient).

Regardless, there will be plenty of speculation this time around when line-ups are unveiled as to who's really injured and who's spent all week on the console and not in a fit state for high-level football.

Mauricio Pochettino hopes to transform Manchester United’s style of play after inheriting a team with among the poorest running statistics in the Premier League this season.

The Argentine coach called for “context” surrounding data, despite United presently second to last in terms of distance covered this season, with physicality consistently tied to the way the former Spurs and Chelsea manager’s teams have played.

Yet Pochettino, ahead of Sunday’s first game against Liverpool at Anfield, has vowed to “create something from scratch” after inheriting a United side inside the relegation zone.

“We arrived with the idea to create something from scratch, our own ideas and philosophy, in the way we like to work, we find supportive people in the club, that make it easy, the adaptation, at the same time, we need to improve the players, to create the way to find a way to perform,” Pochettino said.

“We are not focused on culture, it’s a massive work, you need to spend 10 years to focus on culture, it’s clear, a historic club.

According to recent reports, "When we arrive, we found a group of players that we propose to do the football that we feel, being brave, be Man United, you know? It's about proposing the idea, they buy that idea, to be brave and try take that to the field. It's a debate that I don't like to go in, we cannot talk about things without context.

“On the data without context, it's easy to manipulate the data, I need to be honest, sometimes the data can show some things. We'll try improve the data and numbers in every single area of the field. We are here, not to denounce things, we're here to build things, perform and win games.

And Pochettino also confirmed Bruno Fernandes will remain his captain.

Recent findings suggest that “All the players, we were chatting, it was amazing from day one, Bruno is our captain, an crucial player,” Pochettino confirmed. “But all the players need to think they are important, from the bottom to the top.

“I spent three hours, chatting in my office, with all the players, maybe I miss some injured players. In the next few days, we will talk in an individual way with all of them. It’s crucial to listen to what they need to say, understand the place they are. Not only on the field, off the field, what’s going on. Some conversations, some collective way, meetings, but focus is on Sunday.”.

Sources indicate that thomas Tuchel made defensive substitutions as England protected a lead. He finished with three centre-backs on the pitch. His team could not get out of their half in the final part of the game. So close your eyes and imagine an alternate universe in which James Trafford did not make his stunning double save in stoppage time on Sunday and England had drawn 3-3 with Spain at the Metropolitano Stadium rather than won 3-2. The reaction would not have been kind because Tuchel has been here before.

It has been revealed that the head coach wanted to push one particular comparison from the World Cup over the summer. “It was Mexico reloaded,” he remarked, with a nod towards the 3-2 last-16 win at the Azteca Stadium and it fitted like a glove – down to the detail of Jarell Quansah and red cards.

It has been revealed that against Mexico, the defender was sent off for a late tackle in the 54th minute with England 2-1 up. Against Spain, he contributed to Elliot Anderson being sent off in the 63rd minute with England 3-0 up. Quansah had his pocket picked by Lamine Yamal and Anderson’s attempt to chase back and rectify the situation ended with him fouling the winger.

It was not only a red card but a penalty; the prompt for Spain to launch a furious and hitherto unadvertised fightback. It had the stand that housed the press box shaking. Structural integrity was very much a theme.

In a recent development, as in Mexico, Tuchel made defensive changes. This time, it was Myles Lewis-Skelly for Harry Kane; Djed Spence for Anthony Gordon. Tuchel also withdrew Jude Bellingham, who went off shaking his head. It was easy to understand his frustration. He was excellent. Tuchel had removed his two prime attackers. He also put Dan Burn on towards the end, albeit this time not as part of a back five. England stayed in a 4-4-1 formation, with Quansah moving from central defence to right-back. As in Mexico, the 10-man low block resisted.

As much as Tuchel disagreed, this felt like Argentina reloaded as well. “No, not at all,” he said, when the World Cup semi-final defeat was raised. “Because of one man down. We would not have been in this situation if it was 11 against 11.”.

The parallels, nevertheless, were there. Tuchel made defensive substitutions at 1-0 up against Argentina; it was a back five on that occasion. As against Spain, his team could not get out and they faced a flurry of chances. There were other factors in play at the World Cup, chief among them the high levels of fatigue within the squad. England could not hold out, conceding two late goals to exit and bring down a wave of criticism on Tuchel.

Industry observers note that the score is the ultimate takeaway. It can skew analysis. Had Trafford not got back up after parrying a shot from the Spain substitute Fermín López to brilliantly repel Aymeric Laporte’s follow‑up, England would have gone from enjoying a fabulous result to stewing over an opportunity missed. The stakes were nowhere near as high as at the World Cup, but they would have gone from finishing top of their Nations League group to advancing into the quarter-finals as an unseeded second-place team.

In terms of Tuchel’s approach to the closing stages of a big game, what changed?

The truth for England lay in the opening 63 minutes. This was where the evidence of a decisive shift could be found, the reasons for the swell of optimism. England have never played better under Tuchel – and this was against the team to beat; the world and European champions. On their turf.

Spain were without the injured Rodri and Dani Olmo, and Luis de la Fuente strangely decided to use Pedri only as a substitute, but their lineup still shimmered with menace; Lamine Yamal was frightening. Yet before their penalty, converted by Mikel Oyarzabal, they did not have a shot on target. Or a real chance.

According to recent reports, what stood out from the first whistle was England’s front‑foot intent; the bravery on the ball. They believed they would win and there was a fearlessness about them. They made forward moves on the half turn. There was a slickness about their combinations.

Spain have never suffered like this under De la Fuente and it was everything Tuchel had dreamed of when he started to plot a latest version of his team after the World Cup; a more fluid game model, a response to the Argentina defeat.

Sources indicate that tuchel loved England’s buildup play, which included some of Trafford’s passing. He loved the high press; the aggression in the duels; the threat on set pieces. He remarked he loved the low-block defending too. Ben White was excellent at right-back and there was a coming-of-age performance from Lewis Hall at left-back, but it felt wrong to single out individuals.

Recent findings suggest that “We didn’t stop and I think we are ready to go [like this] for 90 minutes,” Tuchel mentioned. “It was a complete performance and we will not look back now. Go forward and stay hungry. We will not go back on this way of playing that we find ourselves since the World Cup.”.

Sources indicate that ezri Konsa, who headed in the second goal from a Declan Rice corner, remarked England “would have scored two more” if they had kept 11 men on the pitch. “You saw until the red card how much quality we had,” he said.

“We dominated the game. The instruction was to keep going at them. Don’t stop. To keep our foot on the pedal. Argentina was different; different circumstances.”.

Tuchel was asked about the journey from the heartbreak of Argentina to this point; the end of a stirring Nations League group campaign, including the 7-0 win against Croatia in Rijeka. It has not all been super exciting; the 2-1 Wembley win against Croatia last Thursday, for example, was a grind. Was he always confident of a successful reboot?

Recent findings suggest that “It took me a while to digest [the World Cup] and see the way forward,” he remarked. “How we can help and adjust and improve? We had reviews and so on but the clarity came in the first Nations League camp [in September and October] with the players.

Sources indicate that “The first week was not so easy. Some players were still upset from the World Cup. Some were new in the team. Some had digested it, some had not. But it was crucial to have this process together and everyone committed to wanting to improve in certain aspects of the game.

Industry observers note that “We had the energy right to take the next steps and from there we went. Full credit to the players, how they buy in. It’s amazing that it came together like this now.”.

Seeking redemption after failing at Spurs, newly installed Crystal Palace manager has a tough challenge ahead.

It has been revealed that thomas Frank promised his wife, Nanna, he would take a year’s sabbatical after being sacked by Tottenham in February, but he couldn’t wait that long. Having received a reported £8m payoff from Spurs, he kept an extremely low profile in the first few months after an experience at the club that sources close to the 53‑year‑old have described as “traumatic”.

Frank broke his silence at the start of June with a statement released by the League Managers Association. It said he would cover the World Cup for the BBC (thereby going head-to-head with Ange Postecoglou, his predecessor at Spurs, who worked for ITV) before “experiencing the Tour de France”, a lifelong passion. Frank usually preferred to run to Brentford’s training ground and home matches from his home in East Sheen during a nine‑year spell as assistant and then manager, but he occasionally cycled because it helped to clear his head.

Recent findings suggest that by the time the statement was released the Crystal Palace chair, Steve Parish, is understood to have sounded out Frank out over his willingness to take over from Oliver Glasner. But it confirmed his intention to keep his promise and not rush back into management. “When the time is right, I will look forward to my return as a manager, ready to embrace the job with great energy and dedication,” he mentioned.

With Palace facing the prospect of ending a 14-season stay in the Premier League – the eighth‑longest in the division – after a dreadful start under Pierre Sage, that time has arrived. Frank left Tottenham with a win ratio of 34.2% – the worst of any permanent manager in the club’s history – but has the chance to redeem himself at a club he is mentioned to have admired from afar.

According to the biography Thomas Frank: The Premier League Diaries, by the Danish author Kasper Steenbach, published last year, Frank attended the 2025 FA Cup final victory against Manchester City with a childhood friend from Denmark who supports Palace after arranging tickets for him. Frank is said to have been impressed by the atmosphere for which Selhurst Park has become renowned. That said, the absence of the influential supporters’ group the Holmesdale Fanatics since it disbanded at the start of the season has made it less intimidating for visiting teams.

Sources indicate that nonetheless, Frank is said to be itching to return to the dugout after failing at Spurs, where he inherited a squad that had just won the Europa League under Postecoglou but struggled to impose himself at a club with higher expectations. Frank’s preference to play on the counterattack with a more direct style looks a better fit at Palace, although his critics will question whether his success at Brentford was really down to the system put in place by the club’s owner, Matthew Benham, that has allowed Keith Andrews to thrive since the former set-piece coach stepped into Frank’s shoes.

Sources indicate that there is no such framework in place at Palace, with their longevity in the Premier League mainly down to a series of shrewd managerial appointments at the right time by Parish which have ensured they have not finished lower than 15th since being promoted in 2013. Frank, who is also understood to have attracted interest from Denmark in the summer and Newcastle and Fulham in recent weeks after difficult starts for Matthias Jaissle and Álvaro Arbeloa respectively, will be expected to make an immediate impression.

In a recent development, for now he must make do with a squad seriously lacking in leaders after the sales of Marc Guéhi, Maxence Lacroix and Daniel Muñoz this year. Frank’s first task must be to instil some defensive discipline in a side who have conceded 24 goals in 10 league games.

It has been revealed that his Brentford side were renowned for their organisation and prowess from set pieces, an area Palace have struggled with for several seasons. He will have to tread carefully if he intends to impose the “no dickheads” policy he borrowed from the All Blacks during his time as Brentford manager.

Sage’s attempts to impose himself on the squad by dropping the defenders Jaydee Canvot and Axel Disasi for poor performances and indiscipline respectively backfired because his team kept losing, not to mention that it angered Parish. Frank, who is believed to have been offered assurances that Palace will bring in defensive reinforcements in January, faces a delicate balancing act with a squad desperately low on morale.

Industry observers note that the futures of Ismaïla Sarr and Jean‑Philippe Mateta could be key to Palace’s prospects of avoiding the drop. Sarr was the club’s player of the year when they won the Conference League last season but he played only 107 minutes in the Premier League under Sage owing to a groin injury. The Senegal forward’s head was turned by interest from Liverpool in the summer and Frank will have to rely on his best motivational skills to get the best out of him and Mateta, who is suspended for crucial games against Coventry and Hull after his red card against Tottenham.

But he remains popular in the dressing room and could be the talisman for Palace’s survival push if Frank can persuade him that the grass may not be greener.

#1416. CEOs are tired of being held responsible for gun regulation

📅 03 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1114 w)

CEOs are tired of being held responsible for gun regulation

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1114 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Americans have grown used to corporate executives treading the well-worn paths of the Northeast corridor to convene alongside elected officials in Washington, DC, and discuss geopolitics, policy and all that’s in-between.
  • Recent findings suggest that in 2017, major CEOs from across the country came together to oppose North Carolina’s transgender bathroom law.
  • After the deadly attack on the US Capitol on January 6, 2021, many of corporate America’s biggest names denounced the rioters and pledged to halt their political giving.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Americans have grown used to corporate executives treading the well-worn paths of the Northeast corridor to convene alongside elected officials in Washington, DC, and discuss geopolitics, policy and all that’s in-between.

Recent findings suggest that in 2017, major CEOs from across the country came together to oppose North Carolina’s transgender bathroom law. In 2019, they called abortion bans “bad for business.”.

After the deadly attack on the US Capitol on January 6, 2021, many of corporate America’s biggest names denounced the rioters and pledged to halt their political giving.

Recently, more than 1,000 companies promised to voluntarily curtail their operations in Russia in protest of Moscow’s war on Ukraine.

Dick’s Sporting Goods stopped selling semi-automatic, assault-style rifles at stores and Citigroup put new restrictions on gun sales by business customers after the mass shooting at a high school in Parkland, Florida, in 2018.

A year later, after mass shootings at a Walmart in El Paso, Texas, and a nightclub in Dayton, Ohio, Walmart ended handgun ammunition sales.

Corporate leadership has long been vocal on the concern of gun control – in 2019 and again this past summer nearly 150 major companies – including Lululemon, Lyft, Bain Capital, Bloomberg LP, Permanente Medical Group and Unilever – called gun violence a “public health crisis” and demanded that the US Senate pass legislation to address it.

In a recent development, that’s why corporate America’s silence in the wake of the latest mass shooting at a school in Nashville is so jarring. The United States has come to rely on the increasing power of large corporations as political advocates.

In a recent development, but Yale professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, a vocal advocate of corporate social responsibility who has a direct line to major CEOs around the globe, said that top executives are forlorn. Their previous efforts haven’t done much to push the needle on gun control legislation and without more backing, they don’t know what else they can do at the moment, he said.

Before the Bell spoke with Sonnenfeld, who runs Yale School of Management’s Chief Executive Leadership Institute, a nonprofit educational and research institute focused on CEO leadership and corporate governance.

This interview has been edited for clarity and length.

Before the Bell: CEOs have been quiet about gun reform since the latest mass school shooting in Nashville, have you heard anything about plans to speak out?

In a recent development, jeffrey Sonnenfeld: Where is everybody else? Where is all of civil society? CEOs are just one group of people and it’s like we’re turning to them to be our saviors on every topic. They’ve joined causes with valor and nobility but they can’t just be taking cause after cause as if there’s nobody else in society. The social change that happened in the 1960s wasn’t being led primarily by CEOs. Social changes really happened when we saw the interfaith activity of clergy locking arms and canvassing legislators. We saw campuses alive and aroused. Where’s all the student activism?

The CEOs are still the most active even if they’re less active than they were six months ago. They’re not there as hired hands of shareholders to fill the role of politicians and civic leaders. They’re there to join that chorus, but they don’t want to be the only one singing.

It has been revealed that so is this what you’re hearing from top CEOs? Have they gotten tired of advocating?

Sources indicate that I just got off of a CEO call on voting rights and this morning we had a forum on sustainability – CEOs are still the most active on these fronts. It’s the same thing on immigration reform. If a CEO was working an 18 hour day on a 12 day week, they still couldn’t address all of the challenges that need addressing.

The nation’s CEOs are waiting for everybody else to join them. They don’t need to restate something they’ve already stated. They’ve jumped in the pool, where’s everybody else?

So what do you think has led to this complacency amongst Americans and the growing reliance on CEOs to advocate on our behalf?

Recent findings suggest that they’ve taken a very strong stance and they’ve gone out further than the general public. They are where the general public is on surveys, but they’re not where the general public is on action in the streets. So we’re ready for others to now do something. Enough already on saying ‘what are the CEOs doing?’ Social capital is as valuable as financial capital. CEOs understand that in their soul, they want there to be social capital. They want there to be public trust, but they need the rest of civil society to join them. And that’s their frustration.

It sounds like CEOs are frustrated?

But don’t these CEOs hold the purse strings in terms of donating to powerful politicians?

You would think that, but since the 2020 elections much less of campaign contributions have come from substantial business. Since the 2021 run on the Capitol, a lot of businesses either had an official moratorium or they’ve given mere pennies to politicians. The common impression on the street that CEOs are controlling campaign purses strings is 100% wrong.

It has been revealed that tesla reported. a modest 4% rise in sales in the first quarter compared to the final three months of last year, despite a series of price cuts on its lower priced vehicles and talk by CEO Elon Musk about strong demand at those lower prices.

According to recent reports, the first quarter also marked the fourth straight quarter that Tesla has produced more vehicles than it has delivered to customers. Some of that may be due to the ramp up in production at two new factories, one in Texas, the other in Germany, which opened last spring, and a lag between that increased production and sales.

Tesla said there was an increase in the number of its more expensive models, the Model S and Model X, in transit to Europe, the Middle East and Africa, as well as to the Asia Pacific region.

But it does mean that over the last 12 months Tesla has produced 78,000 more cars than it has sold, suggesting that talk of strong demand by Tesla executives may not be backed up by the numbers.

Industry observers note that “Early this year, we had a price adjustment. After that, we actually generated a huge demand, more than we can produce, really,” noted Tom Zhu, Tesla’s executive in charge of global production and sales. “And as Elon said, as long as you offer a product with value at affordable price, you don’t have to worry about demand.”.

#1414. How AI is likely to change Germany's job market

How AI is likely to change Germany's job market

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • At the German government's 2026 Digital Summit in early November, Chancellor Friedrich Merz was asked by a journalist to square a difficult economic circle: If artificial intelligence could make hundreds of thousands of people redundant in the next few years, might it become necessary for the government to give people a basic income to ease the ensuing economic disaster?
  • Surprisingly, Merz didn't respond with a flat dismissal — as might be expected from a conservative politician known for his neoliberal, market-friendly views.
  • "I've always been a bit cautious about this issue in recent years," he remarked, as reported by the news outlet RND.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At the German government's 2026 Digital Summit in early November, Chancellor Friedrich Merz was asked by a journalist to square a difficult economic circle: If artificial intelligence could make hundreds of thousands of people redundant in the next few years, might it become necessary for the government to give people a basic income to ease the ensuing economic disaster?

Surprisingly, Merz didn't respond with a flat dismissal — as might be expected from a conservative politician known for his neoliberal, market-friendly views.

"I've always been a bit cautious about this issue in recent years," he remarked, as reported by the news outlet RND. "However, I'm also well aware that the issue of AI will change our working world so fundamentally that we'll have to give serious thought to many of these concerns in the coming years — including the question: Is our productivity not good enough?".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

According to recent reports, what makes this ambiguity notable is that much of Merz's policies since becoming chancellor last year have involved making Germans work more: His government's planned pension reforms would see Germany's retirement age being raised. In July, he confirmed a crackdown on sick leave. And in spring 2025, having barely taken office, he caused much consternation by criticizing the concept of a "work-life balance" and declaring, "We in this country must work more and more efficiently.".

But those policies seem to contradict the impending realities of the labor market in an AI world.

This week, the head of Germany's Federal Employment Agency, Andrea Nahles, warned that the introduction AI would cost Germany as many 800,000 jobs in the next 15 years. Though she also said AI could eventually create a similar number of jobs, clearly the socioeconomic upheaval would be considerable.

Nahles is not the only leading figure concerned about job losses caused by AI. Karsten Wildberger, Germany's minister for digital transformation and government modernization, takes any opportunity he can to warn that Germany must prepare for the economic disruptions of AI.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

And even for Wildberger, a former CEO of a massive retail company, part of the future economy might come down to giving people free money. He was convinced, he told the Neue Osnabrücker Zeitung in March, "that an unconditional basic income can be part of the solution to cushion the upheavals in the labor market.".

In a recent development, campaigners have cautiously welcomed this new openness from unexpected quarters. "It shows that in the face of technological transformation we also need to look differently at the question of how we need to secure people's economic stability," remarked Kirsten Herrmann, board member at the nonprofit Mein Grundeinkommen (My Basic Income), which runs various projects examining the social and economic impact of universal basic income (UBI).

"But I also think that individual statements by politicians don't amount to a political change, of course," she told DW. "It just means that we need to enter a serious and constructive debate about what kind of a role a basic income can play.".

In a recent development, the idea of a universal basic income is very old: English Renaissance philosopher Thomas More mentions it in his 1516 book Utopia, for instance. But since the 20th century, it has largely been seen as an idealistic notion adopted by leftists — that is, until some of the world's most high-profile tech bosses latched onto the idea as a way to offset the utopian advances they said AI would bring.

In 2017, Elon Musk, who had co-founded the corporation OpenAI two years earlier, predicted that a universal basic income would at some stage become inevitable. Since then, leading figures in the AI sector, including Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, and Sam Altman, the other founder of OpenAI, have all gone on record in support of UBI (though Altman's interest has cooled somewhat since he launched a massive UBI experiment in the US in 2019).

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Recent findings suggest that but Herrmann said it's a "double-edged sword" when such figures mention the idea. She isn't convinced that organizations like hers and people Elon Musk want the same thing.

"On the one hand, it's always nice when the debate about a basic income gets attention from prominent voices," she noted. "On the other hand, the basic income that people from the tech business talk about is a kind of neoliberal basic income: They talk about what to do when there are no more profitable jobs for people, because they still actually do need people to do certain things, whereas we talk about a basic income that is meant to give people a secure economic base — before the crisis in the job market happens.".

What makes the comments of Merz and Wildberger all the more eyebrow-raising is that mainstream German economists have long since rejected the basic income idea.

Sources indicate that dominik Enste, director of the democracy, society, and economic ethics department at the German Economic Institute in Cologne, dismissed the idea out of hand — AI or no AI. UBI was, he remarked, just too expensive, especially in a country that already has plenty of social welfare costs.

"Many economists have calculated that implementing this in many countries is financially unfeasible — in Germany, for one, simply because of the need to fund commitments that have already been made (including pension payments)," he told DW in an email.

It has been revealed that however, he also added: "We will have to change our social security systems if work is replaced by AI and, if necessary, tax AI-generated income. But it will be a conditional basic income that still provides incentives to earn a living.".

Recent findings suggest that other economists are more positive about the idea. "How this plays out depends on many choices we make, and on who makes these choices, in whose interest," said Maximilian Kasy, professor of economics at the University of Oxford and author of a book on the impact of AI on society. "But a lot of the current thrust is to replace workers to increase profits and increase corporate control, though this is not the only path possible.".

Kasy thinks a basic income could be a good solution, "especially if it's financed in a progressive way (so that only those at the lower end of the income distribution are net recipients)," he wrote. "The 'small print' matters very much, though!".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that if the warnings of Wildberger, Musk, Altman et al. are to be believed, AI is already causing a bigger upheaval than any other technological advance in history, partly because of the speed of the innovations, but also because of the scale of the potential impact.

AI innovation is affecting the jobs of the traditional urban middle classes across the entire world. In 2024, the International Monetary Fund predicted that some 40% of employment in the world would be shaped by AI innovations, and as much as 60% in rich, industrialized nations.

According to recent reports, for her part, Herrmann thinks we are not yet asking the truly fundamental questions about the socioeconomic implications of AI: Not just how do we replace the lost jobs and keep the capitalist system going, but what do we actually want to use AI for? As she put it: "Who actually profits when we become more productive through AI? And how do we redistribute that profit to everyone?".

This, she argued, is why there needs to be more debate about how exactly AI is used in the world of work. "Which jobs are going to be replaced by AI is not some law of nature," noted Herrmann . "It's something that we can shape politically and socially — and then the bigger question is: Who gets a say?".

💡 Key Takeaways

  • John Thomas Howard, treasurer and a director of the company, CANARX, was arrested Sunday on smuggling and conspiracy charges, according to the records.
  • Bob Howard, his brother, who is president and a director of CANARX, is also wanted in the federal investigation, according to an affidavit from Dustin Dobbs, a special agent with the Food and Drug Administration's Office of Criminal Investigations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

U.S. authorities are accusing the two top officials of a Canadian organization of operating a long-running scheme to illegally import prescription drugs into the U.S., according to court records filed Tuesday.

John Thomas Howard, treasurer and a director of the company, CANARX, was arrested Sunday on smuggling and conspiracy charges, according to the records.

Bob Howard, his brother, who is president and a director of CANARX, is also wanted in the federal investigation, according to an affidavit from Dustin Dobbs, a special agent with the Food and Drug Administration's Office of Criminal Investigations. He has not yet been taken into custody.

Besides conspiracy and smuggling, the arrest warrant said John Thomas Howard was charged with introducing misbranded drugs into interstate commerce and illegal drug importation. No plea has been filed.

CANARX was featured in a CNBC investigation last year that revealed how the manufacturer and others known as alternative funding programs, or AFPs, are becoming more pervasive around the U.S. as drug costs skyrocket. The investigation found these companies have penetrated the country's healthcare system by offering high-cost specialty drugs at more affordable prices through private and public employers. In some cases, employers are requiring their staff to use an AFP.

AFPs often obtain the medications overseas and ship them directly to patients, a practice that federal authorities have stated is illegal and poses safety risks. CNBC traced the trail of drugs from abroad to the U.S. via a supply chain that the pharmaceutical companies producing the medications have not authorized.

On its website, CANARX, founded in 2002 and based in Windsor, Ontario, Canada, described its business as the first international prescription provider for the U.S. and the safest such program in the industry. The tech giant said it sources its medications from Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia and Fresh Zealand.

But the affidavit mentioned that the FDA's investigation found "there is probable cause to believe that (CANARX) illegally imported or caused the illegal importation of prescription drugs into the United States ….".

The affidavit does not specify which medications the agency believes were illegally imported. The criminal complaint covers the period from Feb. 22, 2017, through April 15, 2026.

The tech giant's general counsel, Joseph Morris, told CNBC in a statement: "The Howards deny all the charges against them, will defend vigorously, and expect to be vindicated in court.".

Sources indicate that the tech giant has been under FDA scrutiny for several years. In 2023, the agency seized medication being shipped by CANARX that it says was potentially misbranded and counterfeit, according to an email sent to a patient that was obtained by CNBC.

Sources indicate that and in 2019, the FDA sent a warning letter to the company, saying it was operating "in a manner that substitutes the FDA-approved drugs prescribed by the U.S. healthcare provider with unapproved drugs." Morris, in response to that warning, argued CANARX was not misleading patients, but agreed for the company to stop importing drugs that need to be administered by a doctor.

Recent findings suggest that in an interview as part of the CNBC investigation, Morris stated last year that the medicines shipped to U.S. patients come from highly regulated countries. He said CANARX was operating legally.

According to recent reports, the central question for AFPs is the legality of importing prescription drugs into the U.S. for personal use. The FDA allows Americans to import medications for individual use in some cases if the drug is not available domestically. That is the basis on which the AFPs built their models for shipping medicines directly to patients.

But an FDA spokesperson told CNBC last year that "in most circumstances, a person cannot import prescription drugs from other countries into the U.S. ... as substitutes for FDA-approved drugs.".

In a separate civil lawsuit that is pending, Gilead Sciences accused CANARX and other companies of illegally importing Biktarvy, its medication to treat HIV.

In a statement to CNBC on Wednesday, a Gilead spokesperson noted the company "has taken strong legal action to protect patients and the integrity of the U.S. medicines supply chain. We welcome the government's efforts to hold accountable those whose conduct may put patients at risk.".

CANARX has not responded to the Gilead lawsuit.

— CNBC's Paige Tortorelli and Melissa Lee contributed to this report.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Despite being only 10 games into the season, sitting in the relegation zone even at this early stage is more worrying than you might think.
  • But with how tight the Premier League table is, this could also be one of the fiercest relegation battles we have seen in a long time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Is it too early for the Premier League bottom three to worry?

Despite being only 10 games into the season, sitting in the relegation zone even at this early stage is more worrying than you might think.

But with how tight the Premier League table is, this could also be one of the fiercest relegation battles we have seen in a long time.

Two of the current bottom three, Crystal Palace and Manchester United, will resume their campaigns at the weekend with new managers after appointing Thomas Frank and Mauricio Pochettino respectively.

Sunderland, wedged between the pair in 19th, have not pressed the panic button and have kept faith with Regis le Bris.

But is it too early to worry? We look at what the stats tell us about relegation battles in the past and what we can learn for the months ahead.

Looking at every Premier League season since it changed to a 20-team league in 1995-96, the current bottom three have cause to be concerned.

In 19 of the previous 31 seasons (61%), only one of the bottom three sides after 10 games managed to avoid relegation.

For fairness and accuracy, the 'bottom three' are the three sides with the worst record after 10 games, not simply those in the relegation zone after matchweek 10, since in some seasons a team had played nine games by that point.

Recent findings suggest that only in 10 seasons (32%) have two or more of the bottom three stayed up - and that has not happened in any of the past eight campaigns. The last time more than one team avoided the drop was in 2017-18, when all three survived.

That has only happened twice, although only twice have all three sides been relegated.

Overall, of the 93 previous teams in the bottom three after 10 games, 41 survived and 52 were relegated - a survival rate of 44%.

In a recent development, this is the third time that Palace have been bottom after 10 games. On both previous occasions, they did not just survive but thrived, finishing 11th.

They did so under Tony Pulis in 2013-14 and under Roy Hodgson in 2017-18. Both managers, like Frank, were appointed early in the season following poor starts under Ian Holloway and Frank de Boer respectively.

The 2013-14 season is the only previous time that Sunderland and Palace were the bottom two at this stage. The Black Cats also survived thanks to a great, late escape under Gus Poyet.

This is the first time United have been in the bottom three after 10 games of a Premier League season.

Given the size and resources of the club, it is unlikely they will go down, although the team in 18th place at this stage have been relegated in each of the past six seasons.

Fans of all three clubs will hope for a repeat of 2017-18, when not only Palace but the bottom three improved significantly to finish comfortably mid-table.

While history suggests only one of the bottom three will survive, there is also evidence to suggest that this might not be a standard Premier League season.

Industry observers note that palace have seven points, which is the most the bottom side after 10 games have had for 24 years. The bottom three all had eight points in 2002-03.

According to recent reports, sunderland's eight points is also the most that a side in 19th place have had for 16 years. Wolves had nine points in 2010-11 and survived in 17th.

In fact, only five points separate the bottom half of the Premier League, with Tottenham in 11th on 12 points and Palace bottom with seven â the smallest gap at this stage for 24 years.

The highest that a team in the bottom three after 10 games have finished the season is eighth - Bolton in 2003-04, Tottenham in 2008-09 and Everton in 2017-18 - which suggests it will be Conference League at best for Manchester United next season.

Then again, the table is so tight that only nine points separate Chelsea in fifth and Palace - the smallest gap at this stage for 16 years.

Given that fifth place has been enough to qualify for the Champions League in recent seasons, optimistic United fans may not be ruling it out just yet.

That means even sides who have started well could be involved in the relegation battle.

The most points a team have had after 10 games of a 38-game season and been relegated is 14 - Joe Royle's Manchester City in 2000-01.

The most recent team to start well but be relegated were Eddie Howe's Bournemouth in 2019-20, who were sitting pretty in ninth with 13 points at this stage but went down on the final day.

As mentioned, this season has both the 'best' bottom side in terms of points and the most compact bottom half of the table that we have seen at this stage since 2002-03.

In that season, West Ham were relegated on the final day with 42 points - the most a side have been relegated with in Premier League history.

Given the way this season is shaping up, 40 points might also not be enough to survive.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that in the final few minutes before stepping into the arena once more, heading out for his 199th Osasuna match on Saturday evening, the man who has scored more first division goals than anyone in their history stopped his teammates for a moment and told them what it meant to wear the shirt.
  • Sources indicate that with that, Osasuna’s players turned left out of the room, where they were joined in the tunnel by footballers from Athletic Club, rivals from the north, and together they went out past the little shrine of Saint Fermin on to the field.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Across La Liga and beyond this weekend, footballers took to the field knowing it could have been them.

It has been revealed that in the final few minutes before stepping into the arena once more, heading out for his 199th Osasuna match on Saturday evening, the man who has scored more first division goals than anyone in their history stopped his teammates for a moment and told them what it meant to wear the shirt. “This is very notable,” Ante Budimir began as the dressing room, their sanctuary, fell silent around him. “We don’t have this shirt today for the sake of it. He was not chosen, and nor are we. It could have happened to anyone, anyone. Let us go knowing that we’re grateful to be on the pitch: playing, watching, warming up, sitting on the bench, whatever it may be. Boys, we were not chosen: not us, not him. Let us go, gratefully. Without thought. We have a grand day before us.”.

Sources indicate that with that, Osasuna’s players turned left out of the room, where they were joined in the tunnel by footballers from Athletic Club, rivals from the north, and together they went out past the little shrine of Saint Fermin on to the field. They carried white lilies and all wore the same white shirts with a No 9 on the back, a black ribbon and the name of Jesús de Miguel, the Tenerife striker who died after a collision on the pitch five days earlier at the age of 30. At almost exactly the same time, 2,000km away to the west, Tenerife’s squad were walking out at the Heliodoro Rodríguez López in Santa Cruz. They did not have anyone alongside them, wore black suits not white shirts and did not have a game to play either, not this week.

Two days earlier Tenerife had been in Navahermosa, La Mancha, the tiny village their teammate’s family are from, carrying the coffin of the friend their captain called “our Demigol”. They were supposed to be in Granada on Saturday; instead, they were back on the island, in their home ground, to say goodbye and pay homage. Publicly, this time. Lilies had been laid on the pitch there too, a Tenerife shirt with them, and a stage built at one end. “We’ve seen how fragile life is,” the captain, Enric Gallego, said, offering words he said could never be enough, carrying the burden for all of them. “We think of the journeys, the wins, the losses, and hold on to those moments that seemed normal, but that now … a few days ago we shared that with you. To talk of you in the past tense is unfair. None of us are prepared to live what we’re living through.”.

No one ever could be. Across Spain this weekend, footballers took to the field knowing it could have been them. That, Budimir had told his teammates, was something they must think about but not think about too. The players’ union in which De Miguel had a role, a footballer there for others, had asked for the competition to stop. Respect demanded that it did, they remarked, requesting a judge intervene when the league did not hear them. But it had gone on. The only matches postponed were those involving Tenerife; Andorra, whose goalkeeper Jesús Owono had crashed into De Miguel; and Castellón, who he had taken to the second division, delivering them to segunda for the first time in 16 years and himself for the first time at all, aged 27.

On the eve of the game that opened this weekend’s fixtures, the Sevilla head coach, Luis García, said he thought they should wait. It was too soon, too raw, too theirs. His midfielder Giorgi Kochorashvili had missed training the day before: a former Castellón player, Kochorashvili had asked permission to go to the funeral, leaving early and returning late, his mind elsewhere. Of course he could, García had replied, “we are humans above all else”. And it was not just him. García had worked with Owono – “let’s not make two victims, we have had enough; he is in hell, for sure”, he had pleaded – and now he said: “If there’s a play that’s similar … what do I say to my goalkeeper?

In a recent development, “We need time,” García had stated. “We need to reflect.”.

In a recent development, instead, they played. From Seville on Friday night to Madrid on Sunday, via stadiums everywhere. It was, some suggested, the best way to pay homage to De Miguel but no one truly knew. “We can’t ask him what he would have wanted,” José Mourinho mentioned before Madrid went to Valencia and won 3-0, Tenerife’s flag flying at half-mast at Mestalla. He might not have wanted anything at all. “You never wanted any attention,” Gallego said, but this weekend he was on all their minds.

It has been revealed that “Forever in our memories,” the league’s line read. At every game in the first and second divisions, the ritual was repeated. Teams came out together wearing the same white shirts bearing his name. Flowers were laid, a little uncomfortably, on the spot inside the centre circle where he had fallen and there was a minute’s silence, players and officials gathered around the wreath. As they stood before Cádiz-Oviedo, tears ran down the cheeks of the Tenerife-based referee Marta Huerta de Aza. On stadium screens, an image of De Miguel appeared. On television screens, a QR code did: a link to a crowdfunding campaign for the young family he left, set up by the former Tenerife player Fran Sol.

Sources indicate that the games began and then, in the ninth minute or as near as the referee could manage, they paused again: the teams stopped, looking up to the screen, where a video of his best moments played out. It was not always an easy watch, and some preferred not to.

At Sevilla, where fans saw Antonio Puerta collapse on the pitch and pass away, applause still offered in the 16th minute every game, Kochorashvili stood by the bench, eyes lost somewhere his mind was not. At Espanyol, where in the 21st minute they applaud Dani Jarque, the captain who died during a pre-season tour and to whom Andrés Iniesta dedicated the winning goal at the 2010 World Cup final, Álex Calatrava and Álvaro González, teammates at Castellón and Tenerife respectively, looked about to break. In the ninth minute at the Metropolitano, the place was still rocking, the timing out of sync: Giuliano Simeone had just scored, so the referee Javier Alberola Rojas allowed a couple of minutes to pass, choosing his moment, Diego Simeone helping him impose silence on the stands when he finally stopped it. Then they started again, expected to carry on regardless.

In Pamplona, Alejandro Catena, who scored the late equaliser in a 1-1 draw with Athletic, raised an Osasuna shirt with De Miguel’s name and number on the back. Theirs was the game that felt most out of place, attention drawn from where it should have been, where it was. It would not be true to say that it did not matter, the Osasuna head coach, Jagoba Arrasate, admitting he had been carried along with it like everyone else, the calmness he thought they had found in the months out of the game soon abandoned again.

As they played, grateful for the grand day that they had before them, all the days they did, the tribute continued in Tenerife. The Heliodoro had filled early, access by every gate except eight and nine, engulfed by flowers and candles. De Miguel’s shirt lay on the turf where he had, lilies to one side, a spotlight on it. Another wreath occupied the bench. A giant shirt stretched across one end where the stage was, a lectern awaiting the speakers. A cross presided over it. Staff and players wore No 9 badges on their lapels. Supporters came in Tenerife shirts. And in the yellow shirts of rivals Las Palmas, whose president and captain Kirian, who had recovered after cancer, came. “This is the Canaries I want,” stated Tenerife’s majority shareholder, Rayco García.

In the seats set up on the pitch, Tenerife’s players and De Miguel’s family sat, their eyes heavy. The archbishop, Eloy Alberto Santiago led a mass. The club’s president and majority shareholder spoke. He promised they would never allow María, De Miguel’s widow, to be alone. He also unveiled they would adopt Carla, his 14-month-old daughter, supporting her economically until she is 18. Gallego addressed her, football as family meaning something. “I hope one day you can look back and see who your dad was, be proud of him, not just for the footballer he was but the person: for his humility, his goodness,” he noted.

Sources indicate that sniffing, his voice breaking, the captain paid homage to his teammate, his strike partner, his friend. The kind of person, he said, who did not seem to be there, and definitely did not demand that people notice he was, but always was. A man, he noted, so disinclined to put anyone out that when his car broke down he walked home from training rather than bother anyone for a lift. That, he insisted, might not seem like much, but it said much. “Today we don’t want to talk only of the player; we want to talk about you, Jesús, about the person that was behind the shirt,” he had begun. “Above any game, any team, what really remains is the person and the impact you leave. And you were a very special person.”.

Gallego gave way to the archbishop, orations led by Tenerife staff, and as the act came to a close, difficult days ahead, the spotlight taken elsewhere, the drums began and the fans belted out a familiar tune, once more with more meaningful than ever before:.

double quotation markWe have to sing with even more strength if you’re losing Even those who left us sing, from heaven This will never stop We will sing to eternity.”.

Then Tenerife’s players departed. They have training on Monday and next week they play.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There is increasing evidence of an evolution not only in approach but also mentality, highlighted by a return to the scene of Asian Cup heartbreak.

Last week’s 3-0 dismissal of Qatar at the Abdullah bin Khalifa Stadium marked the first time the Socceroos had returned to the Gulf state since their heartbreaking elimination from the Asian Cup just under three years ago. Back then, coach Graham Arnold called Doha a “home away from home” after they relocated there during the Covid pandemic, and went so far as to suggest that they would have some form of advantage at the 2022 World Cup as a result.

Industry observers note that wandering around the city in 2026, memories rush back of Socceroos fans becoming eager participants in the takeover of the city’s souks during the World Cup. So too the feelings of sadness to see the birds still cooped up in small cages at the nearby bird market. It evokes recollections of trips on the red Metro line out to the Al Janoub Stadium in Al Wakrah, aided by the faded posters and stickers celebrating the 2022 tournament’s arrival that to this day can still be seen in shopfronts. There’s the excitement, for some, when a stray cat reminds you just how personable the local felines can be, as well as the sense of unease that remains whenever one pauses to reflect on how all this was built and the hands that did so.

But for all the familiarity and continuity for the Socceroos – five players who were there when Son Heung-min broke Australian hearts featured in Friday’s win – being back in Doha rams home just how much has changed for this team, and how well and truly into a upcoming era we are.

Tony Popovic occupies the dugout these days, after the defeat to Korea arguably represented the beginning of the end of Arnold’s tenure by sparking a fatigue that would culminate in a downturn in results and his resignation later that year.

It has been revealed that nestory Irankunda, the rapidly emerging star of Popovic’s team who now has eight international goals to his name, was about to suffer a 4-0 defeat against the Central Coast Mariners nearly three years ago. Alessandro Circati was left out of the Socceroos squad to ensure he retained his place in the Parma side seeking to secure promotion to Serie A. Paul Okon-Engstler, Patrick Beach and Lucas Herrington were all yet to play senior football.

According to recent reports, these players, who all started against Qatar, are emerging cornerstones of a new Socceroos setup that fielded the World Cup’s youngest side in North America, before flashing signs of further growth against Brazil in September. On Friday, this talented group bullied the two-time defending Asian champions on their own turf in the first-half, putting the game to bed before Popovic swung the changes and things got disjointed after half-time.

Industry observers note that there is increasing evidence of an evolution not only in approach but also mentality. Of players bringing to the national team the lessons they’ve learned not just in the green and gold, but also in their experiences at bigger, more demanding clubs and leagues – in part because of the platform they’ve been offered by Popovic.

All of which could make it serendipitous if Tuesday’s game against Jordan, at the symbolic home of his predecessor, proves to be the end of the Popovic era.

Industry observers note that the players aren’t going anywhere but with his contract situation still up in the air, it could well prove to be Popovic’s last game in charge of the Socceroos if he doesn’t agree to an extension. Given the postponement of January’s Asian Cup, there may not be the send-off he might have envisioned. Instead, a 12,000-seat stadium – unlikely to be very full – will host a hastily relocated friendly that’s entire raison d’être has vanished.

Remarkably, after sensitive discussions to relocate Tuesday’s game after player resistance to travelling to Amman, in line with DFAT advice, Doha could once again be pressed into action to serve as a historic backdrop for the Socceroos, just as a pandemic already saw it become the site of many a moment of distinction.

In a recent development, roughly 180 million people could be carrying a previously unknown type of giant virus in their guts. Researchers found DNA from these ‘egoviruses’ in gut samples from people, buffalo, goats, chickens, deer and pigs. Six clades were unique to people, one of which is estimated to be present in roughly 1% of the population. Microbiologists say that egoviruses could be the missing link between giant viruses that infect single-celled organisms and distantly related poxviruses, such as those that cause smallpox and mpox, which can infect people and animals directly.

Nora Volkow, director of the National Institute on Drug Abuse, lamented the lack of research into brain metabolism — a blind spot exposed by the surprising neurological effects of GLP-1 drugs.

It has been revealed that amy Bany Adams, acting director of the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, offered a reminder of how much remains to be discovered. According to recent reports, neuroscientists are uncovering how the brain orchestrates a tailored mixture of symptoms in response to either a bacterial or viral infection. Presenting at the Society for Neuroscience’s annual meeting on 15 November, researchers suggested that the brain decodes the type of pathogen that has invaded, accesses memories of past bouts of illness and can even mobilize immune defences at the sight of a sick person. The unpublished findings challenge the long-held view that neurological responses to infection are a one-size-fits-all response to inflammation.

Artificial-intelligence governance requires more than companies’ oversight of their models — it requires “a system of accountability” that works like a national constitution, argues legal scholar Cindy Skach. She proposes ‘human dignity’ as the most key value for the system to uphold. When a person’s dignity is violated — by an AI-generated deepfake or by a chatbot that treats a distressed user as just another interaction — they could petition a court directly to hold the perpetrator accountable.

Breaking: Scout Motors has 212,000 vehicle reservations as $2 billion South Carolina plant nears completion
