An 18-year-old who has played at two major international tournaments and the division’s top clearance maker from last season also feature.

A tricky, exciting, quick and versatile midfielder, Azeez has proven himself in the Championship with Millwall over the past two seasons and now deserves a chance to test himself in the top flight.

Brighton had been chasing him for a while and struck a deal on deadline day for a very reasonable reported initial £12.5m, rising to £15m. If he can make the step up and produce anything like his second-tier form, he’ll be a steal.

Recent findings suggest that he is a high-volume producer at the sharp end of the pitch, constantly making things happen that threaten the opposition’s goal, but standing out most for his crossing. He ranked top of the Championship last season for open-play crosses (227) and expected assists from crosses (6.71 xA).

In a recent development, he also ranked fourth for dribble attempts (131), ninth for shots (95), sixth for chances created from open play (58). He created good-quality chances, too; only two players created more big chances than he did (18), and he ranked fourth for expected assists. His 9.12 xA alongside only seven assists suggests he may benefit from playing alongside better finishers.

A hugely exciting prospect. Despite being 18, Mbaye has significant and noteworthy experience under his belt. Last year he made six appearances, including in the final, for Senegal at the Africa Cup of Nations and this summer he made four appearances at the World Cup. He has also played in two Ligue 1 title-winning campaigns, including 2024-25, when he became the youngest player in PSG’s history to start a game, and won the Champions League in both of those seasons.

Industry observers note that he is a dribbling and ball-carrying menace, who always looks as if he’s about to do something special. Among players to play at least 900 minutes in Ligue 1 last season, he was 11th for carries (moving at least five metres with the ball) per 90, with 20.0, and 12th for progressive carries (moving at least five metres upfield with the ball) per 90, with 10.3. Most of the players above him in both lists are defenders, who naturally have more space to move into.

In a recent development, he was third for take-on-ending carries, or running with the ball for at least five metres before attempting to beat an opponent with a dribble, with 2.9 per 90. And he also has end product to boot. He scored at Afcon and the World Cup despite limited minutes and his 0.45 goals or assists per 90 for PSG last season is not to be sniffed at.

It has been revealed that danso had a pretty impossible task over his two years at Tottenham. He was the back-up to the first-choice centre-backs Cristian Romero and Micky van de Ven, playing intermittently on both sides of central defence in dysfunctional teams jumping between styles of play, and he very rarely played for any consistent run of games.

He was unfairly compared with the players he was replacing for much of his time there, but the truth is he was always reliable enough. He excelled, however, when Romero got injured during the run-in last season and he was called upon in Spurs’ time of need as they scraped clear of relegation.

He may not be the best on the ball – though he is hardly terrible – but he is an excellent deep defender. Among those to play at least 1,000 minutes in the Premier League last season, Danso ranked first for clearances (8.2 per 90) and headed clearances (6.3), and was fifth for aerial duels won (4.8 per 90).

According to recent reports, he could thrive at Sunderland, who spent more of their out-of-possession game time in a low block than any other team in the Premier League last season (25%). Danso could be perfectly at home in this setup, paired alongside the player he beat into second place for clearances and headed clearances: Dan Ballard.

It was always said during Pep Guardiola’s time at Manchester City that attackers had their wings clipped in terms of individual freedom, limited to playing within the parameters of the manager’s meticulous gameplan.

Industry observers note that but dribbling ability became increasingly important in the final years of his reign, with Jérémy Doku and Antoine Semenyo on the wings and Rayan Cherki in between. Doku (162) and Semenyo (144) ranked first and second for dribbles attempted in the Premier League last season, with Cherki ninth (111). They also ranked first (84), fourth (59) and eighth (51), respectively, for dribbles completed.

Recent findings suggest that with the deadline-day addition of Ndiaye, City have gone in even harder on dribbling ability under Enzo Maresca. The Senegal international ranked second for dribbles attempted (136) and dribbles completed (73) in the Premier League last season.

It has been revealed that fernandez-Pardo’s versatility is a major attraction. He’s comfortable playing off the left and cutting in on to his right foot, or as a No 9. Although not the bulkiest, he has explosive pace and promises to be a threat in behind.

According to recent reports, the Belgium international is arguably at his most threatening when running with the ball because he does so with such purpose. His 122 carries progressing the ball at least 10 metres upfield in Ligue 1 last term were bettered by only seven players, several of whom were defenders.

On top of that, he ranked top for carries into the penalty area (69) and seventh for carries ending with a shot or chance created (39).

In a recent development, fofana appeared to be enjoying a swift rise in 2024-25, only for a serious ankle injury to massively disrupt his development in 2025-26. Sunderland will be hoping they can get him back to the levels shown the season before last, when he was a real livewire on Lyon’s left flank.

According to recent reports, he contributed nine goal involvements (five goals, four assists) in 1,586 minutes in Ligue 1 in 2024-25, averaging one every 176 minutes. Only eight forwards (900+ mins) averaged more expected assists per 90 (0.25).

The most eye-catching aspects of his game, however, were his dynamism and pace. He could be difficult to stop once moving, and this made him a very useful outlet. Among Ligue 1 forwards (900+ mins), his 16.6 carries per 90 ranked him sixth, and he moved up to third for progressive carries per 90 (11.5).

Fofana is direct, exciting and has significant potential. He is a player Sunderland could make a profit on if he reaches the levels previously expected.

Industry observers note that andrés arrived to bolster Brighton’s midfield options after Carlos Baleba’s exit to Manchester United. Although a different type of midfielder to the Cameroonian, Chema is another with vast potential.

In a recent development, A product of Real Madrid’s academy, Chema joined Stuttgart last summer. During his sole campaign in the Bundesliga, he was in and out of the team but caught the eye at the base of their midfield.

It has been revealed that comparisons have been made to Rodri because of his physical attributes and nominal role as a holding midfielder. He doesn’t have anything like the same influence in possession but Chema is tidy on the ball.

Recent findings suggest that it’s what he offers defensively that is most notable, however. He’s been broadly praised for his anticipation and reading of the game, ranking second among midfielders (900+ mins) since the start of last season for interceptions per 90 in the Bundesliga (2.3).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Is Germany's economy back on the up?
  • At the 2026 Mechanical Engineering Summit in Berlin this week, the mood was sullen.
  • The mechanical and plant engineering sector was the backbone of German industry for decades.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Is Germany's economy back on the up? The answer to that question depends on your perspective.

At the 2026 Mechanical Engineering Summit in Berlin this week, the mood was sullen. "A year ago, I said here: We are angry. Today I must say: We are stunned," Bertram Kawlath, president of the Mechanical Engineering Industry Association (VDMA), said in his opening remarks on Tuesday.

The mechanical and plant engineering sector was the backbone of German industry for decades. It once employed more than a million people; now 15,000 positions are being cut every month. Production has shrunk about 20% since 2018.

Kawlath criticized the federal government's infighting and lack of reform, as well as what the companies consider a continued high bureaucracy and tax burden.

Sources indicate that "[We are] stunned by the whitewashing in so many government statements. Stunned by the increasingly visible decline of our country as a business location.".

According to recent reports, german Chancellor Friedrich Merz promised quick reforms and a rapidly noticeable economic upswing when he took office in May 2025. A year and a half later, reality has caught up with him.

Merz's coalition of his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), its Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union, (CSU), along with the center-left Social Democrats(SPD), keeps running into trouble. In addition, there are crises and wars. The German economy is facing more headwinds than seldom before, Merz said in October at the German Employers' Day conference in Berlin.

Given the circumstances, small successes are even more meaningful. "A heartfelt thanks for the good news you bring," Merz said when he received the autumn report of the Council of Economic Experts in Berlin, which predicted economic growth of 1.3% for 2026 and 1% for 2027.

According to recent reports, the economic experts have a German government mandate to independently analyze business activity and make recommendations for economic policy. Earlier this year, they were much more pessimistic.

"The German economy has recovered quicker than expected from the energy price shock sparked by the war in Iran," remarked Monika Schnitzer, chair of the expert advisory board, explaining the prognosis. "We see a significant economic recovery, driven by surprisingly strong exports and high government spending.".

According to recent reports, the chancellor, who celebrated his 71st birthday on November 11, spoke of "encouraging signals" in his address. "The economy in Germany is slowly on the rise again. Considering the many crises in Germany, it was not totally expected that we would manage that.".

In a recent development, but these improved prospects do not change the long-term problems. An ageing society means the bills for pensions, health and caregiving are constantly rising.

At the same time, the number of working-age people who finance these services is sinking. That puts increasing pressure on the public purse. According to Berlin's financial planning, social welfare costs, defense and interest on debt will account for 80% of the spending in the federal government's budget.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

"We must realize that in the long term the expected revenues in the federal budget will not be enough to cover the planned expenses," Schnitzer warned. The growth rates are far below what is needed to secure the same level of prosperity as previous decades in the long term.

"To grow out of this budgetary predicament, we would need levels of economic growth which we haven't experienced in Germany for the past 50 years," she said.

The government is currently in final deliberations over its 2027 budget; spending upwards of €555 billion ($615 billion) is planned. Because revenue won't be enough to cover it, the government is planning to take on more than €118 billion in new debt. Adding the debt-financed special funds for infrastructure and the military, the new borrowing adds up to almost €204 billion.

According to recent reports, the economic experts have warned that if Germany continues with this path, the debt-to-GDP ratio could rise to 100% by 2040. This ratio indicates how high the national debt is in relation to annual economic output. At the end of 2025, it was 63.5%.

In a recent development, germany is the only country of the world's leading democratic industrialized nations (G7) to still hold a AAA rating, the best possible credit rating in finance markets. It signals to investors the smallest possible default risk for German government bonds. "I want it to stay that way," Merz emphasized.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that however, taking on less debt will not be simple. "A reduction in debt-based financing presents policymakers with a consolidation task of historic proportions and will require tough decisions," said Schnitzer. The belt-tightening must, however, be designed to enable growth. Some recommendations include reducing environmentally harmful tax benefits — like the energy tax breaks for diesel fuel.

The so-called "mothers' pension", a pension subsidy for older parents, should be revoked, stated the experts. Tax increases could become necessary in the medium term, for example with value-added tax.

"The burden should be shared fairly between generations and societal groups," Schnitzer said.

According to the chancellor, the experts' message has been received. Solid state finances are an matter in Germany but also throughout the European Union. Merz noted there needs to be a consolidation course, adding that politicians have a duty to the younger generation. Reforms are needed, especially when it comes to social security systems.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Economic researchers are setting their hopes on increasing companies' productivity. Put simply, productivity describes how much a company can generate with its employees, machinery and resources in a set time.

Sources indicate that according to the Council of Economic Experts, there is enormous variation even within the same industries. In Germany, the top companies are up to five times as productive as the weakest enterprises.

In a recent development, if the less productive companies caught up, economic growth could increase significantly, it said in the report. "Newly introduced technologies and business models could drive peak productivity and allow new highly productive companies to develop.".

In a recent development, but innovations need capital. It's here that the Ifo Economic Research Institute sees considerable deficiencies.

New evaluations show that German universities produce significantly fewer successful business startups than their counterparts in the United Kingdom or United States. For example, for every 1,000 students, about 14 venture capital-backed founders emerge from the vicinity of Stanford University each year. In Cambridge, the European leader, it's 3.5. In Munich, by contrast, it's only 0.5.

There continues to be an abundance of inventors and tinkerers in Germany, especially in mechanical engineering. However, the message from the industry summit in Berlin was that for renewed success, labor costs must come down. Suggestions included longer working hours and more flexibility for employers around job protection.

Sources indicate that the intention was not to cut employees' wages and salaries. However, a upcoming study by the German Economic Institute commissioned for the German Mechanical Engineering Industry Association showed that extending the working week by an hour alone would increase real gross domestic product by 1.5% in the coming five years.

Latest Update: Retailers are turning to entertainment to win shoppers’ attention

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1073 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that legacy retailer Gap Inc.
  • It was a newly created role as the company tapped former Paramount executive Pam Kaufman to helm its entertainment, content and licensing platform.
  • Industry observers note that "Beloved brands have value beyond the products they sell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that legacy retailer Gap Inc. made an unconventional hire earlier this year: a chief entertainment officer.

It was a newly created role as the company tapped former Paramount executive Pam Kaufman to helm its entertainment, content and licensing platform. Gap has since rolled out major campaigns, partnering with bands like Just Your Type and building on the success of last year's ads with girl group Katseye.

Industry observers note that "Beloved brands have value beyond the products they sell. Consumers identify with them, trust them and want to be part of their world," Kaufman told CNBC in a statement. "The key is authenticity: Every extension has to reflect what the brand stands for and give its fans a meaningful fresh way to experience it.".

She remarked it's part of a broader goal to emphasize what Gap calls "fashiontainment," a strategy to blend retail and entertainment to better align with consumers. Gap is part of a growing cohort of retailers investing in entertainment and experiences both in-store and through exclusive online content to drive engagement.

Recent findings suggest that "Brands are stories, and we are the storytellers," CEO Richard Dickson remarked at the Goldman Sachs Global Consumer and Retail conference in September. "I think you could see that come to life when you look at some of the work that we've done, putting our brands in the center of culture and cultural conversation.".

In another blending of retail and media, Mattel made waves a few years ago for its "Barbie" movie, building on the intellectual property of a decades-old fan favorite and drawing in massive box office success. At the time, Dickson was president and chief operating officer of the manufacturer, witnessing firsthand the sectors' intersection before departing for Gap.

"I think the post-Covid consumer attitude around shopping certainly evolved a lot," mentioned Bryan Eshelman, who leads the retail practice at consulting firm AlixPartners. "It has gone from shopping as a fulfillment task to shopping, in many instances, more as an entertainment form.".

Between experiences in physical stores and media campaigns featuring exclusive content, Eshelman remarked, retailers are getting more creative about the ways they're driving engagement and marketing.

"Community, at the end of the day, is one of the key ways to drive loyalty, so I think retailers of all types are trying to tap into some sense of community, some sense of lifestyle, some sense of belonging that's beyond the product that they offer," he noted.

Branded entertainment has been around for a long time. Procter & Gamble made headlines in the 1930s for helping to coin the term "soap opera," and companies have for decades created media campaigns to draw in customers.

But with the rise of social media, content creation and short-form offerings, experts said audiences are becoming hungrier than ever for something latest and original.

The retail and entertainment intersection is happening at a time when intellectual property is becoming more valuable than ever, according to experts.

As consumers encounter more marketing than ever, the companies that will win the battle for attention are the ones that can "cut through all of the noise," noted Alex Michael, senior managing director at investment firm LionTree.

According to recent reports, "The hardest thing to find and to get is audience these days," Michael told CNBC. "IP, in that sense, is the most valuable thing out there, and only becoming more valuable because it's attached to audience.".

Recent findings suggest that at the same time, he noted, the way IP is distributed is broadening to include video, audio, short-form, long-form and live event content. Consumers are also redefining their loyalty to brands, which means companies have to "play much earlier in the consumer journey" than they have in years past to secure their trust, he said.

The trend is also likely helped by executives who have worked in both retail and entertainment: Gap's Kaufman came from Paramount, for example, and Dickson and Skydance co-CEO Ynon Kreiz held top roles at Mattel.

In a recent development, "The gray areas have never been more pronounced as to what is classically defined as retail or media or entertainment or live events," Michael said. "People who have cross-sector expertise are increasingly more valuable because you can't be defined by a single vertical, especially as things change so quickly.".

Still, there's room for newer players, especially with the studio landscape rapidly changing, said Sean Akaks, the CEO of SonderCo, an agency that partners brands with celebrities and entertainment properties.

According to recent reports, "I think it's a really interesting time for nontraditional players to be making content because you're seeing this massive consolidation of these legacy entertainment companies," he said. "I think there are just more open lanes for independent creators and also brands and anyone outside the traditional studio system to create content.".

That's where retailers might tap creators, Akaks remarked, because they can use their platforms to reach consumers directly.

"I do think there's a world where we're going to see creators and brands sort of co-creating IP that maybe they're owning together," he stated.

Once those companies get consumers into the store, they're also leaning into experiential retail, making shopping a more immersive experience than it otherwise would be, like Dick's Sporting Goods offering interactive activities and simulators in its stores.

According to data from AlixPartners, companies investing in experiential retail such as Coach and Ralph Lauren saw close to 10% year-over-year increases in consumers' average basket size.

"The idea that retailers would potentially invest in some distributed electronic content to help drive traffic, and then when you get there, it's experiential — it really goes into the kinds of flywheels that entertainment companies are also trying to build and grow," stated Jeff Goldstein, co-lead of the media and entertainment practice at AlixPartners.

In a recent development, yet, the entertainment that retail brands are developing is only one piece in a larger puzzle to retain customers and attract newly introduced ones. Translating that into tangible sales growth isn't necessarily a given.

Recent findings suggest that "The basics of having great product in stock at a transparent price that feels like value is not swept away by animatronics," AlixPartners' Eshelman said. "The fundamentals are still there, and if you're going to have a good retail proposition, you need to have that balance. You can't mask bad product at a bad price with no inventory with glitz and glamour.".

Lowe’s Home Improvement grew the old-fashioned way, working its way up from a single, small, family-owned North Carolina general store founded in 1921. But the Lowe’s hardware store empire is plenty significant these days. A tool-filled Lowe’s superstore is now about as big as a New York City block. The focus is mostly on appliances and tools for the home DIYer, rather than large building contractors. I like to pop in for grill and griddle tools or just some propane. But you can also buy a pre-finished door complete with the frame—or the lumber, sanders, routers, and saws you’d use to make your own door, including the hinges and the wood stain. It’s easy to get lost in the endless aisles if you love the smell of plaster and wood dust, but it’s easier to find the best Lowe’s deals on the website. This roundup includes Lowe’s daily deals, a promo code, and a Lowe's offer code for 40% off appliances, plus info on the Lowe’s rewards program and military discounts.

With winter promptly approaching and temperatures dropping, now is a great time to stay indoors and tackle the home improvement projects and upgrades you’ve been putting off. Shop the Lowe’s Black Friday sale to save on upcoming projects and home upgrades. You’ll find deals on appliances, tools, holiday decorations, grills, bathroom essentials, kitchen upgrades, and more.

With Lowe’s Deals, you can get up to 35% off select major appliances. During this Lowe’s Deals sales period, you can save up to $2,000 when you bundle select KitchenAid appliances and an additional $100 on select Whirlpool and Maytag laundry pairs. Plus, there are hundreds of select and best-selling appliances like refrigerators, dishwashers, microwaves, ranges, freezers, and more.

Industry observers note that it’s no secret that kitchen and bathroom remodels are the most costly home improvement projects any homeowner can take on. For those bigger (and much more costly) renovations, Lowe’s is helping you save more the more you spend. This means you can get up to an additional: 10% off when you spend $750-$1,999, 20% off when you spend $2,000-$4,999, and 30% off when you spend over $5,000. This Lowe’s savings on kitchen and bath program is ideal for homeowners doing a complete room reno, potentially saving thousands of dollars over the course of the project.

According to recent reports, if you’re planning major work this year or just like to putter around, it’s probably worth picking up a MyLowe’s Rewards Program membership. Each eligible purchase accrues points that pay out in $5 increments of in-store credit at Lowe’s. Like many loyalty programs, you get more benefits the more you spend at the store, including free shipping on all purchases, including small ones, member-only discounts, and point boosters for better discounts.

Recent findings suggest that there are three membership tiers, depending on what you buy. One large appliance might already qualify you for the highest tier of rewards, at which point you might as well. These are the three tiers, based on the total cost of what you’ve bought at Lowe’s in the past year. Bronze ($0-$499): $35 minimum for free shipping; 1 point per $1 spent. Silver ($500-$1,999): Free shipping; 1.25 points per $1 spent. Gold ($2,000+): Free shipping; 1.5 points per $1 spent.

Industry observers note that for contractors, there’s a separate MyLowe’s Pro Rewards Program that offers Lowe’s in-store credit in $1 increments for every 100 points earned. (Points expire in half-yearly increments, on June 30 and December 31.) Benefits include member-only deals, volume discounts, free standard shipping in the contiguous United States, and a 20% paint discount after an annual spend of $3,000 or more. Other benefits include analytics and spend reports, online order quoting, and purchase authorization for specified crew members.

In a recent development, all verified active military, veterans, and military spouses are eligible for a 10% discount on full-price items—meaning items don’t have to be on sale to qualify. This is available through what Lowe’s calls the Everyday Military Discount program. When you enroll, you also get an immediate upgrade to Silver status in the MyLowe’s Rewards program, which means more rewards points per dollar and free shipping on all orders in the contiguous United States.

Industry observers note that get a free Silver status upgrade instantly when you enroll in our Military Discount program and validate through ID.me. MyLowe’s Rewards Silver status members receive free standard shipping (excludes AK and HI) and earn more points per dollar.

According to recent reports, another way to get 5% off items you need regularly is to set up a Lowe’s subscription. This is good for items ranging from cleaning products, air and water filters, lawn care, pet goods, plumbing, and batteries. Shipping is free, and delivery happens automatically.

You may not realize that Lowe’s has a Lowest Price Guarantee policy, which means that if you find a lower price on an identical item, Lowe’s will match the competitor’s price. All you need to do is chat with a Lowe’s employee in-store or call 1-877-465-6937. Plus, the Lowest Price Guarantee includes the price of the item(s) plus shipping or delivery costs.

HSBC's top execs face tense shareholders calling for a breakup

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • HSBC’s top brass defended their strategy Monday to frustrated shareholders in the lender’s largest market, as Europe’s biggest bank continued to face calls to be split up.
  • At an informal shareholder meeting in Hong Kong, Chairman Mark Tucker and CEO Noel Quinn took questions from investors on challenges ranging from how the bank was approaching demands for an overhaul of its business to its purchase of Silicon Valley Bank’s UK arm.
  • In prepared remarks, Tucker and Quinn each reiterated the board’s recommendation that shareholders vote against a resolution on the docket for its annual general meeting in May that would force the bank to come up with a proposal to spin off or reorganize its Asian business — the lender’s main source of profits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

HSBC’s top brass defended their strategy Monday to frustrated shareholders in the lender’s largest market, as Europe’s biggest bank continued to face calls to be split up.

At an informal shareholder meeting in Hong Kong, Chairman Mark Tucker and CEO Noel Quinn took questions from investors on challenges ranging from how the bank was approaching demands for an overhaul of its business to its purchase of Silicon Valley Bank’s UK arm.

In prepared remarks, Tucker and Quinn each reiterated the board’s recommendation that shareholders vote against a resolution on the docket for its annual general meeting in May that would force the bank to come up with a proposal to spin off or reorganize its Asian business — the lender’s main source of profits.

HSBC's biggest shareholder reignites debate about breaking up the bank.

Tucker stated the board was unanimous in its opposition to the resolution, stating plainly: “It would not be in your interest to split the bank.”.

He noted the board had previously reviewed a range of options for restructuring the bank, and concluded that such alternatives would “materially destroy value for shareholders,” including dividends.

“Our strategy is working,” Tucker told the room of more than 1,000 shareholders. “Our current strategy is moving dividends up.”.

HSBC has been facing calls to separate its Asian business from the rest of the bank over the past year.

Shareholders in Hong Kong — where HSBC is a mainstay of many retail investors’ portfolios — contend that the London-based lender’s performance has been dragged down by its businesses in other regions.

Quinn addressed those complaints head-on Monday, saying “our profits in Hong Kong and the UK are no longer being dragged down by underperformance elsewhere. The group is performing well as a whole.”.

Pressed later by a shareholder on the glitch, Quinn said a breakup of the bank would result in “significant revenue loss” because much of its business relied on cross-border transactions.

Recent findings suggest that investors have also been unhappy with HSBC scrapping its dividend in 2020, at the request of British regulators. They argue that if the lender cordoned off its activities in Asia, it would no longer have to expose Hong Kong shareholders to requests in other jurisdictions.

Christine Fong, a district council member in Hong Kong, said she represented about 500 small shareholders who had been affected by the dividend cancellation.

“Street hawkers, taxi drivers or teachers — they all relied on the dividend to pay for their regular expenses, like mortgage, insurance payments, school fees,” Fong told CNN.

“That’s why, three years ago, what HSBC did upset those small minority shareholders.”.

Fong has now joined calls for shareholders to vote in favor of the proposal for the bank to spin off its Asian business, despite the lender bringing back its dividend in 2021, albeit at a lower level.

Ken Lui, an activist shareholder in Hong Kong who put the resolution together, doubled down on his call for support ahead of the meeting Monday.

The resolution will require 75% of votes to be passed in May, but “nothing is impossible,” he told reporters outside the meeting venue.

Lui, who mentioned he personally held a stake worth 100 million Hong Kong dollars ($12.7 million), laid out aims for his team to focus on “targeted outreach to institutional shareholders to present our case and gain their support.”.

His group will also canvass 18 districts of Hong Kong “to tell HSBC shareholders that they finally have a chance to speak for themselves and protect their rights through voting,” he added.

HSBC is also facing pressure from its largest shareholder.

Ping An (PNGAY), China’s biggest insurer, holds an 8% stake in HSBC and has backed calls for the bank to rethink its structure.

In a series of remarks made public by the Chinese firm last November, Huang Yong, chairman of Ping An’s asset management arm, mentioned “we will support any initiatives including a spinoff that are conducive to improve HSBC’s performance and value.”.

Since then, the insurance giant’s views haven’t changed, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The source told CNN that Ping An has been calling for HSBC to explore a reorganization, with an eye on boosting its valuation and simplifying its regulatory obligations around the globe.

The insurer has not recommended a specific path forward but will support any initiatives, including a spinoff of its Asian business, that could boost its stock performance or value, the person added. Ping An did not immediately respond to a request for comment on how it planned to vote at the upcoming general meeting.

Recent findings suggest that HSBC’s leaders were also asked Monfday why the bank had scooped up the British unit of SVB following the stunning collapse of its parent in the United States. The purchase was made for £1 ($1.20) last month, just days after SVB had folded.

Critics have questioned HSBC’s ability to perform adequate due diligence on SVB UK’s customers because of how swiftly the deal came together.

It has been revealed that “Did HSBC look into the clients of SVB in detail? Say, the financial statement — whether they can pay back the loan?” said Fong.

HSBC buys SVB's UK business, ending 'nightmare' for British tech.

It has been revealed that quinn and Tucker defended the acquisition, calling it a good business opportunity that allowed the bank to gain hundreds of innovative startups as customers. They pushed back on the notion that management hadn’t had time to carry out proper due diligence.

Tucker also weighed in on recent tumult in the banking industry, saying he did not expect an “immediate impact” on HSBC.

“After the collapse of a number of smaller regional banks and the takeover of Credit Suisse, the share prices of all banks have been suppressed,” he noted.

In a recent development, but he said he did not believe such developments represented “a systemic risk” to the sector. “I do expect a period of uncertainty” before nerves settle, he added.

#1368. How to turn impostor syndrome into a superpower

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1652 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nature ↗ Open Full Page

How to turn impostor syndrome into a superpower

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1652 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that impostor syndrome — a fear of being less competent than people think — is common in researchers.
  • In 2021, Kwabena Boahen Asare found himself in at the deep end when he joined a skin cancer laboratory to gain hands-on research experience.
  • Recent findings suggest that for Asare, who was a first-year undergraduate student at Dartmouth College in Hanover, Newly introduced Hampshire, at the time, it was an exciting but daunting prospect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that impostor syndrome — a fear of being less competent than people think — is common in researchers. Credit: Gandee Vasan/Getty.

In 2021, Kwabena Boahen Asare found himself in at the deep end when he joined a skin cancer laboratory to gain hands-on research experience.

Recent findings suggest that for Asare, who was a first-year undergraduate student at Dartmouth College in Hanover, Newly introduced Hampshire, at the time, it was an exciting but daunting prospect. Not only was he the sole bachelor’s programme student working alongside senior researchers with years of experience under their belts, he was also the only Black person in the lab. Although Asare’s mentor and colleagues were supportive and encouraging, he felt overwhelmed and out of his depth. “There was a steep learning curve,” he says.

At the time, Asare viewed his struggles as a sign that he didn’t belong in research. This feeling was compounded by the fact that he was surrounded by colleagues who didn’t share his background as a first-generation student from Ghana.

His experience, and those of many like him, is commonly labelled as impostor syndrome — the fear of not being as competent or knowledgeable as other people think, despite objective accomplishments. In a world that often prizes unflinching self-confidence and boldness, impostor syndrome is usually cast as a psychological flaw that the individual needs to ‘fix’. But it can be a natural response to working in a challenging environment or striving towards an ambitious goal, organizational psychologists say.

Impostor syndrome can also be a reaction to systemic bias and exclusion in the workplace, particularly for people from under-represented groups, including women, says Ruchika Malhotra, an inclusion strategist and founder of Candour, a workplace consultancy in Seattle, Washington. The tech giant advises organizations on strategies to create diverse teams and inclusive cultures. One study1 conducted at universities in the United States found that women who work in scientific fields that particularly value intellectual brilliance are more likely to feel like impostors than are their male colleagues.

How I tackled post-PhD impostor syndrome.

How I tackled post-PhD impostor syndrome.

According to recent reports, much of the discussion about impostor syndrome pathologizes healthy self-doubt and shifts the responsibility onto individuals instead of the environments that exclude and marginalize them in the first place, adds Malhotra. “A lot of the ways that it’s been talked about haven’t been constructive,” she says.

Although it comes with drawbacks, in some situations, impostor syndrome can be beneficial. For instance, it can help people be better prepared and more focused, particularly when they have a long to-do list.

“Impostor thoughts are almost like your superpower when things get pretty overwhelming,” states Basima Tewfik, an organizational psychologist who studies impostor syndrome at Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge.

According to recent reports, looking back, Asare notes that his impostor syndrome prompted him to reflect on why he wanted to become a researcher in the first place. It has also made him more conscious of his resilience, how he needs to improve and when to seek help, as well as giving him more empathy. This has made him better able to support younger students and researchers who are feeling out of place. “It became my strength,” says Asare, who is now an oncology researcher and consultant at Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center in Lebanon, Upcoming Hampshire.

Impostor syndrome was first described as ‘impostor phenomenon’ in a 1978 paper on high-achieving women2 co-authored by psychologists Pauline Clance and Suzanne Imes, both then at Georgia State University in Atlanta. They wrote that people who experience this phenomenon “maintain a strong belief that they are not intelligent; in fact they are convinced that they have fooled anyone who thinks otherwise”.

Industry observers note that in the decades since, impostor phenomenon has morphed into a syndrome, even though it isn’t a medical diagnosis, nor is it classified as a psychiatric disorder. A review published in 20233 suggests that around 70% of people will feel unworthy of their accomplishments at some point in their lives. These feelings are even more prevalent in academia, with a 2012 study4 finding that as many as 82% of graduate students experience impostor syndrome to at least some degree. This pattern of thinking often affects high achievers and is associated with lower job satisfaction, hindered performance and burnout. Although some studies, including the 2012 paper, suggest that impostor syndrome affects mostly women and people from other groups under-represented in academia, others argue that it arises in specific situations rather than among particular groups. Relatively few studies have investigated whether commonly cited strategies, such as listing one’s accomplishments and accepting compliments from others, are actually effective.

According to recent reports, impostor syndrome has become a catchphrase in popular culture, with dozens of articles, books and courses describing what it is and how people can overcome it. But in the scientific literature, at least, the exact definition of impostor syndrome, or phenomenon, varies widely. This has created a murky picture of what it really is and how it affects people, indicates Tewfik. “There are a lot of different ways people describe this phenomenon,” she says. The loose definition has made it easy to confuse impostor syndrome, which causes people to make inferences about what other people think of them, with regular self-doubt, which is more of a personal reflection of your own capabilities, according to Tewfik.

‘Maybe I was never meant to be in science’: how impostor syndrome seizes scientist mothers.

‘Maybe I was never meant to be in science’: how impostor syndrome seizes scientist mothers.

Much of the research on impostor syndrome has also used measures that have made it difficult to distinguish from other psychological patterns, such as negative affectivity, a personality trait that is linked to a tendency to experience negative emotions such as fear, anxiety and insecurity, adds Tewfik. This crossover might explain why most studies on impostor syndrome have shown only negative outcomes, such as a lack of career planning and low motivation to lead5. “It’s possible that what we’ve been studying is actually something much more akin to fear,” says Tewfik.

This overly negative slant is exacerbated by the fact that many workplaces, including academic ones, place too much emphasis on self-confidence, states Tomas Chamorro-Premuzic, an organizational psychologist at University College London. One 2024 study6 found that workers who display confidence are perceived as more competent and dominant, irrespective of their actual ability.

If impostor syndrome hinders a person’s ability to work or form relationships, it’s usually a symptom of a deeper matter or clinical condition, such as an anxiety disorder. But feeling like you’re about to be ‘found out’ before delivering a substantial presentation, for example, is usually a sign that you’re being challenged or working outside your comfort zone, indicates Chamorro-Premuzic. “There is a very healthy degree somewhere that we’re not appreciating,” he adds (see ‘A toolkit for working with impostor syndrome’).

In scientists, impostor thoughts can simply be a by-product of thinking critically and approaching things with a healthy dose of scepticism, indicates Samantha Sutton, an independent career coach for scientists in Boston, Massachusetts. It’s also often a natural response to working in a high-achieving, competitive environment or towards an ambitious goal and should be normalized instead of treated as a problem to solve, she adds. “If you’re up against something substantial, you should be scared,” says Sutton. When she communicates this to her clients, they are often relieved to hear that they don’t need to strive for total self-confidence before taking steps towards their goals. “They realize that nothing is wrong,” adds Sutton.

#1363. AI in classrooms: Fighting the great 'dumbing down'

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1435 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

AI in classrooms: Fighting the great 'dumbing down'

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1435 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, jakob is 15 years old and attends a secondary school for more academic students, known in Germany as a gymnasium.
  • In a recent development, "I had a French test today, and yesterday I had ChatGPT explain a lot of the topics to me again," the student told DW.
  • Math, German, English, chemistry and even physics: In one click, the solution or the path to a solution is available thanks to AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, jakob is 15 years old and attends a secondary school for more academic students, known in Germany as a gymnasium. He and his classmates have already been using artificial intelligence-enabled tools, or AI, for the last two and a half years.

In a recent development, "I had a French test today, and yesterday I had ChatGPT explain a lot of the topics to me again," the student told DW. Jakob isn't his real name, because he doesn't want to publicly admit he and many others of his age use AI to do their homework.

Math, German, English, chemistry and even physics: In one click, the solution or the path to a solution is available thanks to AI.

In science, this is called "cognitive outsourcing." Basically, the required thinking is shifted to another device, whether that's a calculator, notepad or a large language model (LLM) like ChatGPT.

There's a difference with AI, though. A notepad or calculator can take over a step or two but rarely the whole thought process. That's not the same for an LLM, which can handle the entire problem-solving process.

Jakob admitted he's also had an AI help him with his homework. "But only when I was really stuck," he insisted. And he's also aware that it can become a problem when AI does all your homework. "The students who get good grades tend not to do that," he explained.

In a recent development, franziska Müller has been a German teacher for several decades and is at the moment teaching senior classes at a gymnasium. Her name has also been changed for privacy reasons.

"They can't even think for themselves anymore," she told DW, complaining about some of her classes.

According to recent reports, even in ordinary classes, some of the students type their questions into their tablets or phones, asking for AI assistance. And should they be called upon in class, she knows that they're reading out the answers that the AI has prepared for them and hoping nobody notices.

It has been revealed that müller believes students these days are less able to comprehend text. "Because they read less and let AI summarize almost everything for them," she said.

Several studies have reached very similar conclusions.

Industry observers note that that includes the latest PISA (Program for International Student Assessment) study from September. PISA, which is run by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, regularly evaluates the abilities of 15-year-old students around the world.

In a recent development, "Students who report using AI chatbots get lower scores in science, on average, than those who don't use AI," Andreas Schleicher, the OECD director for education and skills, wrote in his report in October. "This includes using AI to summarize texts they had to read, conduct preliminary research on a new topic, or draft texts for writing assignments.".

According to recent reports, with participants from more than 90 countries, PISA is considered the largest international comparative study of 15-year-olds worldwide. This year, German 15-year-olds posted their lowest PISA scores in the 25-year history of the study.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

"The connections are complex and depend heavily on how generative AI is used, but the central insight is simple: Just as we don't get fit by watching sports but by doing sports ourselves, learning doesn't come from consuming content, but from the mind's productive cognitive engagement with newly introduced material," Schleicher explained.

Put simply, those who don't exercise their brains risk becoming less intelligent.

US think tank, the Brookings Institution, has already argued that the risks of using AI in education outweigh the benefits.

Its own research, which included young participants from around the world, speaks of students losing "fundamental cognitive and durable skills as they increasingly rely on AI to perform learning's intellectual work," as well as the decline of critical thinking, memory, perseverance and independent judgment.

But what can be done against the power of ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Gemini and Meta AI?

Latest York Mayor Zohran Mamdani has banned the use of AI in public schools up to the eighth grade for the 2026 and 2027 school years — so that's up to about the age of 14 or 15.

Not everyone agrees this is the right thing to do. Julian Hinn, who teaches German to students aged between 15 and 18 in Germany, said class members can still use AI apps on their mobile phones. "And anyone who thinks they won't use it at home is ignoring reality," Hinn told DW.

Germany's annual JIM study, which tracks teenagers' media use and device ownership, supports that view.

91% of young people surveyed in Germany, between the ages of 12 and 19, stated that they use at least one AI application. The study also reports that 74% use AI for homework and learning.

Industry observers note that the last JIM study actually dates back to 2024 so those percentages might be even higher now. Data on AI use in Asia, Latin America and the US from the Brookings study show similarly high figures.

It has been revealed that german politicians have recognized the problem. Although education in Germany is the responsibility of the individual federal states, the so-called Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, or KMK, has been issuing statements on the use of AI since 2024.

The KMK's statements have been rather vague though, saying only that students should be enabled to engage with AI in a critical, reflective and responsible manner.

Teachers and students alike are aware that AI can be a powerful support in the classroom.

"The AIs simply explain things much better than textbooks," remarked Jakob, adding that he'll often get an AI to explain basic concepts to him.

Sometimes teachers can't respond like an AI, Hinn conceded. "The AI ​​can respond much better to the language and needs of the students.".

That's why he thinks it's crucial to include AI in classes, starting from the 10th grade when students are around 15 or 16. Hinn doesn't think it should be introduced before that, when children's basic skills are still being developed.

In a recent development, in more senior classes, Hinn will encourage his students to question the AI critically. "We look at the quality of the solutions," he explained.

Industry observers note that german teacher Müller has also integrated some use of AI into her lessons for older students. But in some aspects of the class, she also bans it altogether so that her students can focus on thinking for themselves.

"I understand very well that it's tempting to use AI," she remarked.

Industry observers note that there are also other problems with AI in education. According to the Brookings study, students with basic skills can use AI to deepen their learning and progress faster.

But for children with gaps in their knowledge, they tend to adopt AI's errors, outsource their thinking and then fall even further behind. In this way, AI can exacerbate preexisting inequalities.

The PISA study notes that children from more affluent backgrounds often have a better start, and AI can widen that gap.

This is called the Matthew effect — the name comes from the biblical verse Matthew 25:29, "for unto everyone that hath shall be given." It basically means that early success in learning leads to better progress in the future, while early struggles equal a growing lag over time.

In the age of AI, teachers have become more motivated to challenge students to think independently and to consider their own personal autonomy.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Hinn, who also supervises the school newspaper, noted: "I always tell everyone, you can use AI but the feeling of having written an article with your own pen is spectacular.".

According to recent reports, both teachers also stress the idea of personal autonomy and responsibility. They believe this affects the students, especially because when they sit exams, they aren't allowed to use any aids or AI. And if they aren't able to solve their own problems, they will fail.

It's during exam time that the students really find out if they can solve those math, English or science problems by themselves.

It has been revealed that müller remarked one of her students recently confessed they were upset after a poor exam result. "He felt he simply couldn't think for himself anymore because of AI," she said.

Tech Report: Eric Trump-backed robot soldier startup can't pay staff after founder borrowed $4.6 million from manufacturer to buy home

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1225 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Foundation Future Industries, a maker of military humanoid robots advised and backed by Eric Trump, failed to pay employees last month as its cash reserves dwindled, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter.
  • It has been revealed that workers have yet to receive paychecks after San Francisco-based Foundation missed payroll on Oct.
  • The situation has particularly angered some inside the startup because its co-founder and CEO, Sankaet Pathak, borrowed $4.6 million from the organization last year to buy a luxury home, money that could have been used to pay workers, the people said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Foundation Future Industries, a maker of military humanoid robots advised and backed by Eric Trump, failed to pay employees last month as its cash reserves dwindled, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter.

It has been revealed that workers have yet to receive paychecks after San Francisco-based Foundation missed payroll on Oct. 30, mentioned the people, who asked for anonymity to speak candidly about a private firm.

The situation has particularly angered some inside the startup because its co-founder and CEO, Sankaet Pathak, borrowed $4.6 million from the organization last year to buy a luxury home, money that could have been used to pay workers, the people said.

Public records show that an LLC that names Pathak as sole principal purchased a $4.6 million Sausalito, California, property with "sweeping, cinematic views" of the San Francisco Bay in October 2025.

A spokesman for Pathak acknowledged receiving a detailed list of the major points from this story on Thursday, but didn't respond to requests for comment. Pathak's previous startup, a fintech firm named Synapse, collapsed in 2024, leaving thousands of Americans locked out of their savings accounts.

Foundation's cash crunch comes at a precarious moment for the company, which Pathak has mentioned is close to unveiling a next-generation, weapons-ready robot that will help the U.S. compete against Chinese rivals. At the same time, Pathak is seeking to raise hundreds of millions of dollars in funding at a $3 billion valuation.

The tech giant has garnered headlines this year for Pathak's claims that his robots could soon take on battlefield tasks in Ukraine or patrol the U.S. border with Mexico. Broadcast interviews and articles about Foundation also include claims that the company has won $24 million in Pentagon contracts.

"What we're about to unveil in the next couple of months [is] going to be the strongest humanoid robot that exists anywhere in the world, including China," Pathak remarked in an April television interview.

Recent findings suggest that that April interview introduced Eric Trump, the son of the U.S. president, as a Foundation investor and chief strategy advisor. It is unclear how large his stake is.

According to recent reports, eric Trump and his brother Donald Trump Jr. have invested in an array of defense firms, including makers of military drones and autonomous weapons. A July Washington Post investigation found that startups backed by investment vehicles linked to the brothers had secured at least $3.2 billion in government business.

"We have to win robotics in the United States of America," Eric Trump said in April. "When you go up and interact with these robots ... they fist bump you, they high-five you, they follow your commands.".

In a recent development, eric Trump's involvement in Foundation drew the swift ire of Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who asked whether Foundation won U.S. defense contracts because of nepotism.

"Eric Trump went on FOX to brag about winning ANOTHER multimillion-dollar contract from the Trump administration," Warren said in an April 23 social media post. "This looks like corruption in plain sight.".

Eric Trump didn't respond to requests for comment. His spokesperson recently told the Financial Times that Eric Trump had "no involvement in Foundation's management, operations, strategic decisions or commercial activities, including the solicitation, negotiation, procurement or execution of any government contracts.".

While the Eric Trump announcement created speculation within Foundation that a Democratic-led Congress may look to investigate the firm, Foundation itself didn't actually win the $24 million in contracts, despite that assertion being widely reported across news outlets.

In a recent development, instead, it acquired Florida-based Boardwalk Robotics in late 2024, and government research contracts won by that firm account for the claim, said a person with knowledge of the matter. Foundation used Boardwalk's robot Alex as the basis for its first robot, the Phantom MK-1, this person said.

Foundation's deal for Boardwalk included performance milestones for the robot that haven't been reached, noted a separate person with direct knowledge of the deal.

In 2024, CNBC reported that letters Pathak sent to prospective investors cited an imminent investment and $300 million purchase order from General Motors, claims the automaker rejected.

Foundation co-founder Mike LeBlanc remarked at the time he was "embarrassed" about the marketing materials.

Insiders fret that Foundation could soon fold if Pathak doesn't secure fresh funding. Pathak has been seeking to raise hundreds of millions of dollars at a $3 billion valuation since at least January.

In a recent development, pathak is Foundation's sole board member, a structure that has raised concerns among prospective investors about corporate governance, remarked the people familiar with the matter. He also owns most of the firm's shares.

That setup allowed Pathak to borrow $4.6 million last year, which he called a short-term loan at the time, the people mentioned. Existing investors are aware of the loan through the company's financial disclosures, the people said.

Industry observers note that "This is what happens in a company with no governance," remarked one of the people. "Are you just going to let it ride into the ground, and you ride off into the sunset?".

Foundation also ran out of cash for payroll in August, though employees only had to wait about two days to get paid after the company secured a bridge loan from an existing investor, the people noted.

Pathak told employees this week in a memo that he was working on sourcing money to pay back wages.

The company was founded in April 2024 by Pathak, Tribe Capital CEO Arjun Sethi and LeBlanc, co-founder of Cobalt Robotics, a maker of autonomous security guards, according to a fundraising pitch at the time.

Foundation went on to hire dozens of robotics engineers and artificial intelligence experts, managing to lure some from Tesla and Amazon-owned autonomous vehicle firm Zoox.

Before Foundation, Pathak was known as the founder of Synapse, a kind of middleman that enabled fintech firms like Mercury, Dave and YieldStreet to offer savings accounts and credit cards with the help of small community banks.

Synapse was a behind-the-scenes player until its collapse left more than 100,000 Americans with a combined $265 million in deposits locked out of their Federal Deposit Insurance Corp.-backed accounts.

While some customers received partial payments during Synapse's bankruptcy proceedings, thousands remain without access to their money after more than two years. A bankruptcy trustee, the former FDIC Chair Jelena McWilliams, noted as much as $96 million in customer funds went missing.

The bankruptcy proceedings concluded last year without uncovering where the funds went; Pathak blamed a banking partner named Evolve, and Evolve blamed Synapse for the mess. U.S. regulators didn't intervene until the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau sued Synapse last year, opening up a $55 million fund for customer relief.

Pathak withdrew $320,000 in loans from Synapse as it spiraled toward bankruptcy in 2024 amid disputes over unmatched ledgers, according to the consultant and independent journalist Jason Mikula.

Federal prosecutors convened a grand jury to investigate possible criminal misconduct at Synapse, The Wall Street Journal reported last year. The Journal report didn't mention Pathak specifically.

The controversy didn't dissuade Eric Trump from investing in Foundation and Pathak, who he called a friend in the April broadcast interview.

It has been revealed that "I walked into his factory, and I couldn't believe what I saw," Eric Trump stated. "I'm telling you, he's doing a phenomenal job.".

Kompany was appointed Bayern Munich manager in May 2024.

Bayern Munich boss Vincent Kompany notes he is "very healthy" and grateful for all of the support he has received as he prepares to return to the dugout on Friday.

The 40-year-old former Manchester City captain was taken to hospital after falling ill while watching the club's second team train last month.

Kompany was diagnosed with meningeal irritation - an inflammation of the protective membrane surrounding the brain and spinal cord.

Speaking at a news conference on Thursday he thanked the club, medical staff, players, coaches and fans for their support.

"It was very intense," he remarked.

According to recent reports, "At the time, it was a latest experience. Looking back, everything went perfectly. I received support right away, from the club and the doctors. I'm very grateful.

"You try to stay calm and wait until you have the results. It was a positive process, all the tests were positive.

Industry observers note that "I have to say, I'm very healthy. We did a lot of tests, and they all came back fine. In those quiet moments, you also try to learn.

"Now I feel very good again and I'm happy to be back with the team.".

While he has been recovering Kompany's assistant Aaron Danks has led the side to four wins and a draw.

"I'd also like to thank the coaching community," Kompany added. "We're always competing, but almost every coach has reached out to me, even if we've played against each other and perhaps argued as well. That's a beautiful thing.".

Bayern, for whom England captain Harry Kane has been in fine form, are top of the Bundesliga, level on points with Borussia Dortmund.

Defending champions Bayern face Cologne on Friday after the end of the two-week international break.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that leaders of several U.S.
  • That was the overall sentiment from CEOs of Rivian Automotive, Lucid Group and EV startup Scout Motors during interviews with CNBC after Democrats' historic midterm election wins.
  • "We've honestly constructed Scout from day one to be in an environment where we're not going to count on, let's say, legislation or count on things that may or may not be there," Scout CEO Scott Keogh, an automotive veteran, told CNBC on Wednesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that leaders of several U.S. electric vehicle manufacturers said they're not counting on increased federal support for their businesses once Democrats gain control of Congress in January, but they said they'll gladly take it if it does happen.

That was the overall sentiment from CEOs of Rivian Automotive, Lucid Group and EV startup Scout Motors during interviews with CNBC after Democrats' historic midterm election wins.

"We've honestly constructed Scout from day one to be in an environment where we're not going to count on, let's say, legislation or count on things that may or may not be there," Scout CEO Scott Keogh, an automotive veteran, told CNBC on Wednesday.

EV makers have had to contend with flip-flopping support from Washington over the years. The Trump administration has ended or rolled back support for climate change initiatives and EVs that were supported by the Biden administration, including an up to $7,500 customer incentive for purchasing an EV.

Legacy automakers such as General Motors and EV startups alike had counted on such credits to help them boost their sales and assist in electric vehicle profitability. But now they don't have that same level of federal assistance.

Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe stated it's his hope that the Democratic-controlled Congress and Republican President Donald Trump can find middle ground to make progress for the EV industry, but Rivian's not counting on that.

"We try not to plan for those sort of things. The reality is it's probably going to have less of an impact than we think," Scaringe noted Nov. 6 following the election results. "I think we're going to actually have a lot of challenges getting things done.".

Fellow EV manufacturer Lucid, which is backed by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, is taking a similar approach.

Recent findings suggest that "You know, they say, 'Initiative for the worst and … hope for the best.' That's all we can say," Lucid CEO Silvio Napoli told CNBC on Monday. "Anything positive, we'll take it.".

The lack of expected support comes as Democrats seem to be more focused on hot topics such as healthcare and data centers rather than climate change and support for alternative energy technologies such as EVs.

It has been revealed that CNBC previously reported that House Democrats blueprint to bring to the floor bills reinstating the enhanced health insurance subsidies that expired under the GOP-held Congress and reversing the Medicaid cuts Trump signed into law last year. They also plan to focus on oversight of the Trump administration and affordability.

Rachel McCleery, executive director of the nonprofit policy advisory Coalition for Reimagined Mobility at SAFE, said she believes affordability concerns also could include the cost of vehicles, including EVs.

Sources indicate that "I fully expect there will be legislative debates over what to do moving forward, including on EV and EV supply chain incentives," McCleery, a former U.S. Department of Treasury senior advisor and Ford Motor policy director, said. "Bringing down the cost of vehicles for U.S. consumers is top of mind for Democratic policymakers, and electric vehicles are a critical aspect of this agenda because of the multiple challenges greater EV adoption solves for.".

Scout's Keogh said if legislators decide to offer any type of support, he would prefer it to be for EV production, which could then have a trickle-down effect on vehicle pricing and help companies amid inflated costs.

"I always prefer it on the production side," Keogh said. "Anything that can drive down production cost is going to, of course, get passed along to the customer.".

Affordability has been a concern for EV adoption as the vehicles typically cost more than traditional models with internal combustion engines.

Sales of EVs spiked last year ahead of the Trump administration ending the up to $7,500 incentive after September 2025, but have since come down from that high.

Industry observers note that cox Automotive reports the average price for a new electric vehicle as of September was more than $54,800, according to the most recent available data. That compared to the average overall industry at just over $51,100 last month.

In a recent development, "Ultimately, incentives can help accelerate adoption, but the industry can't build its long-term strategy around them," Stephanie Valdez Streaty, Cox director of industry insight, noted Friday. "The goal has to be making EVs affordable and compelling enough that they make sense for more consumers with or without an incentive.".

#1343. Can a 'coalition of the willing' create momentum for a fossil fuel phaseout?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1065 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Can a 'coalition of the willing' create momentum for a fossil fuel phaseout?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1065 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, this time last year, as negotiations at the UN COP climate summit in Brazil entered crunch time, there was hope that governments would agree on a clear roadmap for phasing out oil, gas and coal.
  • But instead, after opposition from oil-producing states such as Russia and Saudi Arabia, the conference wrapped up with a watered-down final agreement that did not explicitly mention fossil fuels.
  • Recent findings suggest that as a compromise, summit host Brazil offered to produce a "voluntary" roadmap.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this time last year, as negotiations at the UN COP climate summit in Brazil entered crunch time, there was hope that governments would agree on a clear roadmap for phasing out oil, gas and coal. More than 80 countries backed the idea.

But instead, after opposition from oil-producing states such as Russia and Saudi Arabia, the conference wrapped up with a watered-down final agreement that did not explicitly mention fossil fuels.

Recent findings suggest that as a compromise, summit host Brazil offered to produce a "voluntary" roadmap. At the same time, a group of 57 countries frustrated with the deadlock at the consensus-based UN talks decided to form a "coalition of the willing" to accelerate the fossil fuel exit outside the COP framework.

They held their own summit in April in Santa Marta, Colombia — the first such conference to specifically focus on implementing the transition away from fossil fuels (referred to as TAFF).

Co-hosted by Colombia and the Netherlands, the Santa Marta conference brought together countries including Canada, Norway, Brazil, Nigeria, Mexico, Australia and Germany, as well as highly climate-vulnerable states such as Vanuatu.

The idea was for governments to start developing national roadmaps and working out how to restructure their financial and trade systems to wean themselves off polluting energy sources — an incredibly complicated undertaking, particularly for developing countries dependent on revenue from fossil fuel exports.

Part of their discussions focused on cutting subsidies for oil, coal and gas, as well as supporting people whose livelihoods rely on the fossil fuel industry to find latest forms of income.

A little over six months on from the Santa Marta meeting, representatives from almost 200 countries are holding talks in Antalya, Turkey, as part of the latest UN climate conference.

Countries agreed for the first time in 2023 to transition away from fossil fuels — the main driver behind rising global temperatures. But summits since then have failed to pin down how to implement that pledge.

It's not yet clear whether the Santa Marta coalition will influence ambition at this year's COP.

"I think it's more of a long-term game," noted Chetna Hareesh Kumar, a climate policy analyst at the Berlin-based research organization NewClimate Institute.

In a recent development, she says it's too soon to expect the coalition to have an influence on the negotiations but adds that that could change at future COPs. The grouping could bring more nations on board if, for example, it demonstrates it can be truly inclusive, address the needs of different types of countries and show that a transition is feasible.

One role the group is playing, according to Alexandra Scott, a senior climate diplomacy adviser at Italian climate change think tank ECCO, is "keeping up the political momentum," and showing "that there is this huge group of countries who really want to accelerate this transition away from fossil fuels.".

She says it's also building an invaluable "cadre of knowledge" on how to develop national TAFF intends and deal with barriers individual countries face — like how to secure funding for the infrastructure investments needed for the energy transition.

The Santa Marta group is "really answering a lot of the questions that countries have always had on how on earth do we even start to transition our whole economy off fossil fuels?" Scott remarked.

This expertise being shared and tested in practice can show what such a transformation could look like and the knowledge brought into COP, added Scott.

According to recent reports, since the Santa Marta conference, Germany, France and the Netherlands have released national plans to phase out fossil fuels. While the plans contain no new commitments, experts see them as a positive first step.

Kumar indicates more countries could announce similar intends just ahead of the second TAFF summit in Tuvalu next year. Finland presented its TAFF roadmap in the first week of COP, but analysts do not expect many more countries to follow suit soon.

Another potential boost that could get momentum going is Brazil's recently published global roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels, promised at last year's COP.

In a recent development, the nearly 200-page document seeks to serve as a toolkit for countries shifting from fossil fuels to renewable energy, such as wind and solar. It envisages countries making a phased transition between 2028 and 2033.

The aim, Ana Toni, CEO of last year's COP, told AP, is to break down the transition into "smaller actionable solutions" and help countries make practical progress.

It has been revealed that the roadmap suggests measures tailored to each country's circumstances, including dependence on fossil fuel and financial capacities. "Levers" it proposes include reducing fossil fuel subsidies, expanding renewable energy and cutting methane emissions.

Kumar called it a "customizable" approach that allows every country to take action, regardless of its situation. "The question really is now what countries do with it and how much momentum they can generate," she added.

This year's climate change summit in Turkey — taking place after a series of deadly heat waves in Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people — isn't expected to result in any massive announcements about fossil fuels.

Global renewable energy capacity has surged in recent years, making up a third of the world's power generation for the first time in 2025. But many countries still rely on coal, oil and gas.

A database compiled by the German environmental organization Urgewald indicates that most oil and gas companies worldwide, among them QatarEnergy, Saudi Aramco and Russia's Gazprom, are exploring or developing fresh reserves.

Meanwhile, subsidies for fossil fuels amount to around $920 billion (around €830 billion) per year, according to data from the OECD, but that number is falling.

It has been revealed that one concern Turkey is pushing at the COP conference is electrification. It's calling on countries to endorse the goal of 35% of final energy consumption coming from electricity by 2035 — up from around 20% today.

The pledge has drawn criticism from some circles, though, for leaving open whether that additional electricity needs to come from clean sources.

Ideally, Kumar stated, electrification would be powered by renewables and tied to a goal of phasing out polluting fossil fuels.

"If something like that could make it to the final text, that would be a really good sign for momentum.".
